FIRST NARROWS BRIDGE On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the government in connection with the First Narrows bridge at Vancouver. The contractors are ready to start work, financial arrangements have been made and all that is necessary now is the consent of the federal government. I should like to know if the government has arrived at a decision or is likely to arrive at one in the near future in connection with this matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on more than one
occasion since this session began I have answered questions with respect to the so-called First Narrows bridge. The fairway or entrance to the harbour of Vancouver is very narrow and the effect of placing a bridge over that entrance is a matter of grave public concern. The fact that the city of Vancouver desires that money should be expended to construct the bridge, the fact that private interests are willing to provide capital and the fact that certain points will become more closely connected are all matters of private and semi-public concern. The government has been asked to express approval of the construction of a bridge and the considerations which the government will have to have in mind when arriving at a conclusion are not those affecting private interests, they are those affecting public interests solely. With so narrow a fairway, with water so shoal, with some ships having only eighteen inches of water under their keels when going to sea, the house will readily understand that there are matters of grave public concern that must be considered when determining the particular type of bridge that should be constructed. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) is primarily responsible and I can only say that he has not yet submitted any recommendation to council with respect 
to the matter. Many questions are involved in this matter, not the least of which is the effect of a single bomb dropped by an aeroplane upon the structure and blocking up the harbour of Vancouver and the results which might follow in certain eventualities with respect to our obligations of neutrality or other obligations which may rest upon the state. The government must consider all these problems and the minister who is charged with responsibility is submitting the .matter to council at an early date. In the meantime, I cannot express any opinion as to what action may or will be taken. All I can say is that every consideration which affects the public interest from the standpoint of the Dominion of Canada as distinct from private interests will be considered.
Is the right hon. gentleman aware that the eminent authority, Sir Alexander Gibb, has endorsed this bridge from an engineering point of view?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: His report has been sent to the Minister of Public Works. He deals with the structure as such, its size and character and so on, but he does not undertake to deal with certain other problems with which the government necessarily has to deal.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, June 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Weir (Melfort) for the third reading of Bill No. 51, to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provisions in connection therewith.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking last evening before six o'clock I indicated that I thought I would be able to spend a short time in dealing with one of the statements made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull). I intended to do this not because it was anv different from any other statement but because he seemed to have fallen into the error into which most hon. members have fallen, that is, he believed there was no outstanding relationship between the standardization of farm products and the marketing thereof. This is a very common error. I do not suppose half of the hon. members knew there was such a close relationship between standardization and marketing. At the risk of repeating what a very good authority has said on this subject, I should like to read again the quotations I gave the other day from Major Elliot, the Minister of Agriculture for Great Britain. He said:
Standardization is a fundamental principle of our modern commercial system.
And again:
The commercial advantages of standardization are well known and need not be repeated
here. In this country, as elsewhere, legislation has proved to be necessary to put the standardization of farm produce on a national basis. Here, it has taken the form of the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marketing) Acts, 1928 and 1931.
I pointed out that when the Liberal government went out of power we were almost through with the process of standardization and grading of those commodities which were exported. Here is Major Elliot's last statement:
So the time has come to develop further the policy to which successive governments have already contributed and prepare to rebuild the whole organizational structure of our agricultural marketing.
That makes it quite plain, even to a doubting Thomas, that there is a very close relationship indeed. I dealt with this question in my remarks of Tuesday, and I shall not weary the house by repeating. I want to state that the establishment of this central marketing board plus the standardization of farm products which had taken place up to 1929 is one of the most important features of this marketing bill. Over one thousand cooperatives and other farmer organizations were in existence in this dominion and I should like to show the house what might have been the final different results of these organizations and activities had we had such a body as the central board to collect information and to supply counsel and advice to such farm bodies. If there had been such a body I am sure the disappointing results of many of our farm organizations would have been quite different and much more successful. I referred to the great work done in the early days of the inception of the grange movement. I should like to quote from A History of Farmers' Movements in Canada, by Mr. Wood. If any hon. gentleman would like to extend his knowledge on these matters he could not do better than read this book. He says:
The things for which the grange movement has stood in Canada were set forth in what was entitled its "declaration of principles." This document was a compound from two main sources. Its introductory clauses or preamble-was taken from a general preamble explaining the objects of the Patrons of Husbandry, adopted at the sixth annual convention of the National Grange held at Washington, I).C., in January, 1873. The bulk of the document, however, was formed of selections made from the declaration of purposes of the National Grange, accepted at its St. Louis sessions, February 4-12, 1874, and of which J. W. A. Wright, a California granger, was the leading author.
The preamble to the declaration of principles states that instruction in the art and science of husbandry is to be above all the aim of the

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
Grange in Canada. " The products of the earth," it asserts, "are subject to the influence of natural laws, invariable and indisputable; the amount produced will consequently be in proportion to the intelligence of the producer, and success will depend upon his knowledge of the action of these laws and the proper application of their principles. Hence knowledge is the foundation of happiness." Membership in the grange gives the farmer an opportunity to combine in order to attain his ends. " Unity of action," continues the preamble, "cannot be acquired without discipline and discipline cannot be enforced without significant organization; hence we have a ceremony of initiation which binds us in mutual fraternity as with a band of iron; but, although its influence is so powerful, its application is as gentle as that of the silken threads that bind a wreath of flowers."
Heading the declaration proper is found the motto of the order, to wit: "In essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity." Canadian grangers' ideas on the economics of agriculture are therewith outlined in pithy language. They plan to give added attention to the diversification of crops, and in general to make their farm lands more selfsustaining. With the object of reducing the weight of their exports, grangers will adopt the policy of selling "less in the bushel, and more on hoof and fleece." Knowing too the value of foresight in their industry, they intend to "calculate intelligently on probabilities."
That expression to-day would be "economic planning" under the new order.
And to avoid the influences that have militated against the success of agriculture in the past, the order will "discountenance the credit system, the mortgage system, the fashion system, and every other system tending to prodigality and bankruptcy."
If we had had a central board with the status and importance of government supervision during these intervening years, I wonder how many of all these sound principles would have been preserved to this day. I think there would have been a whole lot of them. But with no guiding hand over them, these bodies scattered all over the face of Canada, exploited by every adventurer who chose to make use of them for his own political and other ends, languished and died on the political reefs and rocks as they have done on other occasions since, as I pointed out on Tuesday last. A great many of the business and social virtues indicated here have been lost sight of not only in Canada but in many other countries, though they might have been retained if we had had a central board such as that established under this bill. Let me repeat this sentence:
And to avoid the influences that have militated against the success of agriculture in the 
past, the order will "discountenance the credit system, the mortgage system, the fashion system, and every other system tending to prodigality and bankruptcy."
The disregard of these prime virtues pointed out in this grange platform has largely been responsible for the economic condition in which the world finds itself to-day.
My right hon. leader reminded us yesterday that the present world situation is nothing new but possibly more world wide. After every great war business depression has existed in great intensity, possibly not on such a large scale as at the present time; but we have always had these depressions after great tragedies like war. Here is an organization which has as the basis of its declaration of principles what I have just read, and I want to read a little more from this fine work:
Upon the question of the business relations of Canadian grangers, the declaration is very explicit. The order holds no enmity to capital; legitimate business must obtain; transportation companies are necessary to agricultural development. On the other hand the grange in Canada is firmly determined to bring producer and consumer more closely together. "We must dispense with a surplus of middlemen,"-
This will be interesting to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with the mass buying and price spreads investigation now going on.
-contends the document, "not that we are unfriendly to them, but we do not need them1-[DOT] their exactions diminish our profits." Any "tyranny of monopolies" would be distasteful to the granger just as he would be "opposed to excessive salaries, high rates of interest, and exorbitant per cent profits in trade."
No hesitancy is shown in repudiating the idea that the grange in Canada has in any sense been established for political purposes.
Every farmers' organization I know of, of a special character like this, for the last sixty years has had in the forefront of its platform the declaration that it had no intention whatever of going into politics, and I believe that at the outset no organization of the kind has had any such intention. In the course of a number of successful years however they begin to feel their oats, if I may say so; they begin to realize their power, having had access as advisers to governments and their advice having been taken and well taken. And there is no objection to political action if it did not put their commercial activities *invariably on the hummer. But finally such organizations plunge into politics, possibly led by only one or two clever platform performers, and that is the beginning of the

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
end. I dealt with that the other day and I will not repeat now what I said then. I would point out however that we have now one most hopeful-looking young people's organization, one of whose slogans is, "Save Canada -save agriculture;" and they would be horrified if anyone suggested to them that they were laying the foundation of another political party. They have no idea of such a thing now. But the fact is that farm organizations nearly always start out like that and end in political action. I am satisfied that all these well-meaning organizations would be *most helpful to governments in an advisory way if they had some central rendezvous or friendly place of concourse in this capital to which they could ask for sound advice. If such organizations had had a retreat of that kind to advise them they would have been saved many a tragedy and disaster. Let me quote still further:
"No grange, if true to its obligations," is the emphatic statement, "can discuss partisan or sectarian questions." It might not call political conventions, nominate candidates, or permit of the discussion of questions on which its members stood divided on party lines. At the same time, the granger must perforce take a deep interest in political issues. It must be his business to do everything in his power to put down "bribery, corruption and trickery" in connection with public affairs. The principles of the order, it was thought, should be of great value in the realm of government, because those principles "underlie all true politics, all true statesmanship."
The declaration states quite candidly that the grange movement in Canada is meant exclusively for the farming population. A barrier must be imposed to the admission of the non-agriculturist, since he has "not a sufficient direct interest in tilling the soil, or may have some interest in conflict with our purposes." But sex distinctions are wholly eliminated within the order; more than that its aim is "to inculcate a proper appreciation of the abilities and sphere of women." While an advocacy of better agricultural education is considered a watchword among Canadian grangers, they desire to obtain better facilities for education all round. "We shall advance the cause of education," is emphatically promised. "among ourselves, and for our children, by all just means within our power."
In the west, in the old Grain Growers' Association, we had an organization almost identically the same as this, and for years the government of Saskatchewan were advised by them on many public issues of the day and took that advice and enacted it into law. But once any such organization goes into politics it becomes a political party like the others after which governments and parties will not be so much disposed to take their advice because they do not know whether such
advice is merely political or quite disinterested as formerly. Let me now turn to another phase of the question.
The central board provided for in this bill plus the farm economics branch established by the previous government is from my standpoint the most important part of this whole legislation. It will supply a continuity, a rendezvous, a clearinghouse, a registration bureau, if you like, of all these bodies from the Atlantic to the Pacific and protect them from the ravages of the twolegged wolves that, as I previously indicated, tear them asunder on occasions by beguiling them into politics.
I come now to a more recent date than back in 1872. It will be noticed that in the bill wheat is specifically provided for, and I think the government should make it quite clear that under present international wheat conditions and agreements this measure cannot very well apply (to local boards in regard to wheat. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) closes the debate, as I understand he will, he should give a frank expression of opinion on that if he looks upon it from that standpoint. I feel those representing the wheat pools in the west are quite well aware of that, but on the other hand many in the west are under the impression that this legislation will work a miracle so far as our wheat is concerned, that there is going to be a sudden transformation, something springing up like the old wheat board of 1919, that will give them continually rising prices. It would be in the interest of the bill, the government and the farmers tc. disillusionize them on that point because it is generally understood that under present economic conditions and international wheat agreements the government must keep close control of the marketing of that product. I express the wish that the Prime Minister, if I am wrong, will make it quite clear what the bill intends in that respect.
A year ago last February I put on the order paper a resolution which I am about to read. Before I did that, the same subject had been dealt with by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). I gave him some support and when this resolution of mine was put on the order paper he gave it some support. In February, 1933, I made the following motion:
Whereas, unemployment, scanty clothing and hunger throughout the land continue to be all too prevalent, and
Whereas, this persistent economic depression not only adds to the growing relief requirements in many centres, but also suhstracts from the number of voluntary contributors, many of

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
whom are now feeling these social efforts growing more and more beyond their capacity to carry,
Therefore, be it resolved-That, in the opinion of this parliament the government of Canada should place a sufficient quantity of our surplus wheat stocks, at the disposal of the Red Cross, welfare bureaus and other similar organizations, to supplement and more fully take care of the food requirements of the unemployed, the poor and the hungry throughout Canada.
And be it further resolved-
This is the more important part of the resolution:
That the government of Canada take such steps as are necessary and expedient to explore the possibility and practicability of selling on long term credits a substantial quantity of our embarrassing wheat carry-over to China, or any other available country where poverty, hunger and misery prevail.
This government for some strange reason seems to have taken it for granted because we are being gradually squeezed out of Great Britain and the European continent by one cause and another, the policy of self-sufficiency on their part being the principal cause,-and the others I do not care to mention now-there was no other market elsewhere. The Prime Minister on the occasion of discussing this resolution made some very nice and I might also say complimentary remarks to the author of it, but he indicated-and possibly this was a fortunate way out-that China was now at war with Japan and under those conditions we could not play favourites. But when the resolution was put on the order paper my recollection is that they were not at war and besides the resolution applies not to China alone but to all the oriental countries where poverty prevails. Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) made a brief reply; at that time he did not think it was necessary to fuss up about this thing; there was not any market there anyway; it was filled; it was described quite graphically how what are usually called commission houses would gobble it all up if we tried to do anything along the lines of barter trading, and anyhow the whole cloud was going to lift soon and things would resume their normal swing in the wheat and other markets of the world. But conditions have been and are getting worse as to wheat carryovers. Has any hon. member during the interim heard anything of this government seeking markets anywhere? They are simply sitting there apathetically and putting the brakes on production instead of doing anything in the nature of trying to merchandise production. I do not want to be too harsh at this time; I have tried to carry through the debate on

this bill in a moderate tone of voice and moderately as to substance so as not unnecessarily to ruffle anybody's feelings, and I intend to continue that course. But if I were in the other humour to-day as I sometimes am, I could pound the stuffing out of the government with respect to their ghastly apathy in the matter of possible oriental markets. I remember in the year 1909 or 1910 when the late Sir William White packed his kit and went off to Japan to see what could be done there to develop our wheat and flour trade, and later on the late Sir George Poster did the same thing. Japan has since become a great wheat flour eating country; and with those millions of people in China who are gradually learning to eat more wheat, instead of selling more we have lost our trade almost altogether with that country. I would like to hear anybody contradict that statement because I was rather hoping they would as I would then have an opportunity of giving the information gently to them. I will put my best ear to my hon. friends to see if they cannot dissent from my statement.

For fear, however, I forget this when I finish my present remarks -and I shall not be very much longer-I would be glad if the Prime Minister would consider the advisability of discussing with the house the international wheat agreement, that is set a day apart, or at least if he would tell us why he did not ask our concurrence in it. When a comparatively unimportant matter like silver, because important as it is it is relatively unimportant in comparison with wheat, was discussed and concurred in at the tail end of a resolution, tacked rather adroitly on to the motion of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), surely a farreaching proposal like this international wheat agreement should have had the concurrence and support of the house before it was put into operation. I just mention this now for fear I might forget it, this being my last chance on this bill to discuss the China situation from the point of view of a wheat importing country.
Unfortunately I shall have to read, again. This is a review of China's wheat trade in 1933 by B. A. Macdonald, assistant trade commissioner. I think it would be nice if somebody would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to come into the chamber because he may not have seen this.

speechtext:
Issued every
Saturday by the Department of Trade and Commerce: Minister H. H. Stevens, M.P.; Deputy Minister; James T. Parmelee. I will read it without comments because it may be capable of explanation; there may be an alibi.
Shanghai, March 16, 1934.-China's imports of wheat in 1933 amounted to 1,181,000 short tons or 39,367,000 bushels valued at roughly Canadian $23,500,000. This is the largest import for any year since the trade first began in 1921, with the exception of the record year 1931 when 1,518,000 tons were brought in. As a result wheat has become the third greatest single import, ranking after rice and raw cotton, and it now represents 6-47 per cent of all imports as compared with 4-87 per cent in 1932 and 6T1 per cent in 1931. The 1933 percentage is the highest yet recorded. Since the London wheat conference estimated world import requirements for the 1933-34 crop year to be 560,000,000 bushels and since China took 39,000,000 bushels in the calendar year 1933, it would appear that this country is now absorbing somewhere between 5 and 10 per cent of world imports, and must constitute therefore one of the foremost of the wheat markets.
The principal features of the year's trade were briefly as follows:
(1)	Australia's continued and increased dominance.
(2)	Argentina's notable participation.
(3)	New Zealand's participation for the first time.
(4)	The complete absence of American and Russian wheat.
(5)	Canada's decreased participation due to the low prices and depreciated exchange of Australian and Argentine supplies.
(6)	The imposition of a duty on wheat and flour for the first time.
(7)	The wheat credit arrangement effected between the United States and China.
And we disappeared off the map, although we had both good wheat and low grade wheat, whichever they desired. Now I should like to read a further brief reference:
The fact that Canada's position declined so greatly in the past three years, just when China's imports increased so greatly, has perhaps partly obscured the potential importance of this market. It is worth noting that if
Canada had in this latter period maintained the average share which she held from 1922 to 1930 inclusive-
Mark that period, 1922 to 1930 inclusive.
-namely, about fifty per cent-she would have sold to China 750,000 tons or 25,000,000 bushels in 1931, 500,000 tons or 15,000,000 bushels in 1932, and 590,000 tons or 20,000,000 bushels in 1933; and in each of those years China would have been the dominion's second or third greatest wheat market.
That is very significant. Where have all the ministers disappeared to? There must be something important in that return that was brought down to-day. It was represented to us by the government that we could not get a look into that market at all, but I am afraid we have been humbugged by this government on this question, though I do not know why. Were they so busy at home looking after price spreads, mass buying and what not, the natural by-products of high tariffs, that they [DOT]could not attend to the maintenance of the Chinese wheat market? They did not need much of a periscope to see that we were losing rapidly this oriental market. What we wanted was new wheat markets abroad, but apparently the government were entirely oblivious to the fact that this market was disappearing from under their noses. I continue reading:
As it was, China was Canada's sixth largest wheat market in fiscal year ended March 31, 1933 (the last year for which statistics are available here), being exceeded by the United Kingdom, Belgium, the Netherlands, France and Germany. The figures for fiscal year 1934-
Listen to this.
-will, of course, show a reduced importance, reflecting the fact that Australian and Argentine wheat almost shut out Canada from the market during that period.
And here they are sitting complacently as though everything was well and there were no more markets to be sought or obtained; as though the only thing to do was to reduce exports, which automatically means a reduction in production. And, if the production should keep up, their only resort in addition to these restricted exports under the wheat agreement is to keep the surplus production at home in the granaries. What a wonderful solution for a number of supposedly sane gentlemen familiar with the requirements of the country. That is what has been done. These wheat agreements have been entered into by the three western provinces, and this government has not seen fit to bring them before this house for concurrence. I am satisfied that the Prime Minister is not strongly behind them; I am sure his knowl-

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
edge of business and of the hunger throughout the world makes this program of lessened exports abhorrent to him. It is a strange thing that the government cannot do better than that, though after much tribulation they were able to work out a marketing bill, the first we have had. In spite of their blundering they have brought about an advance by providing marketing facilities for local requirements, though in my opinion there is going to be great disappointment in this marketing' bill unless the government elucidate a little more as to how it is going to affect our wheat sales. It is not going to do veiy much for wheat under present international agreements. It will help our cattle, I think, but it has its limitations even there unless export markets are secured.
We want access to these markets, any markets, wherever we can make the best bargains in order to dispose of our surplus products. From the government's own figures, if the percentage of total wheat sales to China that existed between 1922 and 1930 had been maintained we would have sold nearly 50,000,000 bushels of wheat more than we did sell. That would have made a big hole in our carry-over. Then, if we had bartered or had sold on long term credits as the United States did we could have sold another fifty million bushels easily, if I know anything about conditions in that country. That would have meant a total of 100.000.000 bushels, practically our entire above normal carry-over by next August.

speechtext: You have been very indulgent, Mr. Speaker, so perhaps you will allow me to say just a word or two in conclusion. Just watch how this act will glide into operation in respect to those commodities and those growers that are ready for it. First there will be the dairy products of the Fraser valley and elsewhere, already organized for years; then the fruit of the Okanagan valley, and then the cattle of the prairies, also organized. With those three well under way the act will be well launched. My only regret is that all hon. members could not have seen it in the same way and so reduced to a minimum the friction that always extends into the highways and byways of the country when a government and an opposition engage in deadly combat over the merits or demerits of such agricultural legislation. Such controversy unfortunately always hampers very much the general acceptance and subsequent administration of the act.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, to some extent I find myself in the same position as the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). At any rate, on second reading we both started from scratch. We both proclaimed our intention to vote for the second reading, because we believed a principle was involved in the bill, and we hoped that the measure might be amended in committee. I believe both of us took the stand that if it were not amended in the direction we each desired-and we were not a unit on what we wanted-we would feel justified in voting against it on third reading. The hon. member for Melville has since announced his intention of voting for the third reading. I find that two days ago he described the bill, as reported at page 3669 of Hansard, as a "Tory distortion of Liberal principles and contrary to what the farmers asked for" and so on. So I assume that he thinks there have been substantial amendments introduced which would justify his intention of voting for it. With that, of course, I have no complaint, because I,have no responsibility for his actions. So far as I am concerned, however, this question arises: Has the bill been changed in any material degree which would require any change of view on my part? In moving the third reading, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) went to considerable trouble and into some detail to point out that the changes were immaterial, and entirely a matter of detail. I do not propose to be guided wholly by his advice or by-

I do not intend to follow the advice of the Minister of Agriculture or the somewhat involved reasoning of the hon. member for Melville through which he has arrived at his conclusion. I propose to examine for myself the bill as amended, and to ascertain whether or not the conditions I wished have been obtained.
More than once the Minister of Agriculture [DOT]asked for cooperation in the handling of this measure. The bill had not been long in committee before he accused hon. members on this side of the house of deliberately obstructing, an action on his part which I think was a mistake. Possibly he may have thought we were obstructing, but I am of the opinion that

Marketing Act-Mr. Neill
much of what he thought was obstruction was really a genuine and desperate attempt to find out what the bill actually meant. There were a great many hon. members on this side of the house-and I was one of them-who had the greatest difficulty in trying to find out what the bill really meant. After having served some considerable time in this House of Commons I must say that I do not think I have ever seen a bill so comparatively short which has been so involved in meaning and reaction, and which appeared to be so difficult of explanation or defence by the hon. gentleman in charge of it.
I believe some justification for the criticism offered by hon. members on this side of the house is to be found in the unusually large number of amendments which were somewhat *reluctantly introduced by the minister in charge. Certainly he did not exhibit any disposition to meet the opposition, unless it was a case of absolute necessity. And, with regard to obstruction, I think that if any members or any body of members in this house had been really opposed to the ultimate success of the bill they could not have done better than to let it go through in the form in which it was originally introduced, because, had they done so and simply thrown the responsibility on the government and said, "There is your baby; carry it to its ultimate destination," it would have been the shortest way to effect the death of that unhappy infant. It certainly would not have proved a monument but would be an epitaph on the gravestone of their reputation. However, the fact remains that the opposition did suggest changes, a number of which the minister accepted.
Moving the third reading the minister said he regretted the fact that he could not follow the precedent, laid down in Great Britain and in one or two other British countries where somewhat similar legislation has been adopted. Again and again he used the argument, the argument which he used so often in committee-in fact it was an answer to almost every inquiry1-that it was necessary to have the bill flexible. If a man is going to climb a mountain as fast as he would like, he does not choose a flexible staff to aid his faltering footsteps, and I am afraid that when the minister comes to defend the bill in the courts of law-as undoubtedly he will have to do, and perhaps before the privy council, because his pride will not allow him to accept defeat in a lower court-I am afraid he will find that his desire to have flexibility in the bill will be but a weak reed upon which to rest.
He has said he cannot support the principles involved in the British legislation. Nobody has asked him to follow the British bill, in detail. But there are certain main principles which apply just as much in one country as in another. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) told us yesterday that truth is not eternal. I differ from him, and I say that there are some main principles of common sense which are equally applicable whether they apply to the British Empire, .to the United Kingdom or to Canada. I am not talking about the details involved in the different conditions existing as to size and area. But there are certain main principles of what I might term common sense which, I suggest, could most certainly be applied.
Of the changes introduced by the minister, I take it that the principal one is in regard to pooling. The hon. member for Yale in British Columbia (Mr. Stirling), a strong supporter of the bill, speaking in the early stages of the debate, in fact he was one of the first to speak, said that he saw-and he must have seen it with the eye of faith -that there was some provision in the bill for pooling. Certain words he indicated he thought would provide for pooling. But he could not find, nor could I find any lawyer who would undertake to risk his reputation by saying that that was what was really meant, nor could it be inferred. I protested and my protest is indicated at page 2257 ol Hansard. Later on an amendment was brought in, but it consisted only of the introduction of one word, " pooling," in the middle of a long and obscure paragraph-so obscure, in fact, that it did not appear to be good English, .and was hardly intelligible. I pointed out that fact, as did other hon. members, and as a result the minister withdrew the amendment, and now subsection 6 of section 4 gives power to conduct a pool, and that only.
The minister refused to listen to suggestions made by me that he accept, at least in some part, the provisions made in the British legislation, whereby pooled money should be earmarked, how it should be paid out; that certain expenses should be paid, reasonable advances made, and finally that the balance should be paid to those who had supplied the product. He refused to do anything of that kind, an improvement which I think would have made the bill noticeably better.
I come now to some of the features which *he refused to correct. I find that in subsection (b) of section 4 provision is made to exempt from any determination or order- and it should not be "determination," because
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

that is simply superfluous-to exempt from any determination or order any person or class of persons engaged in the production or marketing of the regulated product or any *class, variety or grade of such product. I protested strongly against that-and I protest again-that it is absolutely wrong for us to take such action. This is an instance where we could have followed Great Britain. What did Great Britain do? They have said that in their scheme, as it stands, certain small producers would be exempt not from orders to be issued day by day, but from the whole scheme. They do not have to sit up day and *night because of their two cows or eight hens, to see if they come under the shadow of the law. They know they are exempt from the scheme, and I suggest that that is the way exemption should be made in this bill. Instead of that the minister insisted-and the minister alone knows why-upon leaving the exemption to be placed on each individual order. Under these schemes orders may be *issued once a week or once a day; every man has to sit up nights and wonder whether he is exempt from this order or -that order, and the body issuing the order has to exempt him each time. That is an absurd situation. *Relief should have been given by exempting him from the whole scheme, thereby avoiding trouble and confusion. There is the suggestion-and I do not charge the minister with it, but subsequent ministers may be charged -that favouritism may be shown, because it would be so fatally easy just to happen to forget to exempt some political exporter friend from one of these orders, and it might mean a small fortune to him. This cannot be done under the British style.
We now come to section 4 (c) which deals with compensation for loss. I do not think that section was improved by the amendment introduced later on. This is one of the features dangled before the poor man in the street who says, "I think this bill is a step in the right direction." He is told, "You see, *here it states that if you wish to ship stuff to a market and you are forbidden to ship it, you may be compensated." But the amendment kills it. Of course those people are not *told about the amendment which provides that under ordinary circumstances they could not get any compensation at all. If it goes to a country where a quota has been put on and there is reason for the prohibition of export he gets no compensation. There is another clause the wording of which might

be used to prevent him being given compensation under any circumstances whatever.
There was no provision made for what I might call the odd producer with a grievance and a proper grievance, because in a scheme like this there are always bound to be injustices, and the British people very properly provided for a board of arbiters to which an individual producer who felt he had been wronged or suffered an injustice could appeal and get satisfaction. There is no reason in the world why we should not have a system like that here. And the same with regard to the protection of the consumer. Britain has two boards; we have none. Does the difference in the shape or area of Britain compared to Canada make it undesirable to protect the consumer here and highly desirable to protect the consumer in Britain?
The same thing about contracts. Business lives by contracts made far ahead, but the minister would not listen to me when I suggested that as in the British act there should be a clause in this bill protecting contracts legally entered into in good faith before the scheme comes into effect. The minister would not even allow the word "forthwith" to be inserted. As the bill now reads, when these schemes are formulated, they must be published in the Gazette. I suggested that they should be published "forthwith" in the Gazette because I know of cases and I could cite them here, but they are known to members of the house, where a nefarious order in council was put through and not published for weeks afterwards. The minister agreed that it would not do any harm, and I got the support of the Minister of Justice to word the amendment correctly, and then the minister used his majority to vote it down. But these are smaller matters.
There are three special features which I consider of major importance, and on which I shall base my decision to vote or not for the third reading They are these: Section 5 subsection 1, says:
A representative number of persons engaged in the production and marketing or the production or marketing of a natural product-
That is entirely contrary to the British system. The British act does not say anything about marketers. In their scheme it must be the producers. This subsection is open to the widest abuses. The right hon. leader of the opposition yesterday dwelt very fully on that phase of it. He said it was putting into the hands of an occupational group too much arbitrary power to control. He might have gone further and pointed out that under this

Marketing Act-Mr. Neill
section not only might that arbitrary power be used possibly unfairly by the occupational group, but it might be so used by the people who are engaged in the marketing end only of that group. I was willing when the bill was in committee to have the words inserted "production and marketing" to take them both in, but no, the minister insisted upon putting this clause in. It says, and that is what it means, that the control of an industry may be put in the hands of a mere handful of middlemen, wholesalers, brokers, and men of that type who, by a little judicious manipulating of an order, or under section 9, simply with the consent of the minister in charge of the bill, may get complete control of an industry in the hands of half a dozen men who have no more interest in it than that of moneymaking by handling its produce. You can hunt the British act far and near before you will find authority for anything of that kind.
Next with regard to the taking of a poll, which is provided for in section 5, subsection 3. The minister, after considerable pressure, allowed the introduction, of permissive polling, but the British act from beginning to end is full of safeguards and insists that a poll "shall" be taken. It is not left to half a dozen middlemen, nor to the minister to decide under section 9, but it is very fully safeguarded in the British act, so much so that the polling is surrounded with all the safeguards and solemnities, I was going to say, at all events all the formalities that attach to taking a vote at a general election. Just the same care and attention is to be taken in taking a poll of all the people interested in any scheme under the British act. While the minister has recognized the need for the principle by conceding that there "may" be a poll, he leaves it entirely open to the will of the man who happens to be at the head of the department at the moment.
Then we come to section 9. To put it in a sentence, section 9 takes all the powers of all the other sections of this bill together and combines them into one, and gives the whole power to the minister. It means that, and it means nothing less. It even gives the governor in council or the board appointed by the government power, as I brought out by a query in the committee, to buy and sell. They can go into wholesale marketing, and there is no polling about that. The poll is only held out as a little window dressing in these other sections, but is a poll compulsory under section 9? No. Would the spirit of the British people tolerate anything like that for a moment, I wonder?
Those, Mr. Speaker, are three of the worst features of the bill. If they had been amended I would have gone a long way to vote for the bill in spite of other minor objections, but these three are fundamental objections to my mind, and the bill has not been changed, and will not be changed, in these respects.
The minister in introducing the bill said that there were three fundamental principles urgent and necessary for the success of this act, that it should be simple, sound and practical. Simple? Anyone who has tried to wade through this act will know whether it is simple or not. The only sense in which the word simple could be applied to it is that in which my Scotch fellow-members know it is used in Scotland when they say charitably of a poor fellow whose mental progress has been arrested, "Oh well, the poor fellow is simple." In that sense this bill may be called simple.
Sound? It is not sound. Practical? Time will show whether it is practical or not.
I voted for the second reading of the bill with the fond and foolish hope that it would be improved in committee. I did not turn my ears to my friends to my right who were attacking it possibly because they were prejudiced, but rather inclined my ears to my friends to my left and opposite who were supporting it. I was going to listen to them and hear the arguments they advanced. I did listen to them attentively. I have heard or read very carefully practically every one of their speeches, and with possibly one exception, through them all ran the thread of damning and double-damning the bill with the very faintest of praise. Here is a sentence that you find in almost all of them: Well anyhow it is a step in the right direction A step in the right direction, and perhaps two in the wrong direction. Is all this trouble and turmoil worth while if we are only going to take one step in the right direction? Anyway, let us take a chance on it, they say. Well, lots of people have got into trouble by taking a chance, and if we are only taking one step in the right direction; if we are going to take a chance anyway, let us fill up the gaps and minimize the risks.
I would like to quote my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) speaking at page 3968 of Hansard. The hon. gentleman is known to be one of the best speakers in the party to which he belongs, and I always listen with interest to his speeches. They are always carefully prepared and couched in the most appropriate language to make his meaning very clear. I think I can say without
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

any disrespect

I do not think he will object -that he is also known to be a very loyal and strong supporter of any measure the government brings down. I listened to his remarks very carefully, feeling sure I would get support for the step I was inclined to take. One of his remarks was (that it was a step in the right direction, and I have already alluded to that. Then later on he states that the amendments cleared up many points introduced in so vague a manner as to be capable of complete misapprehension and complete misinterpretation. That does not agree with the minister who says that the changes have been immaterial. Then we find the hon. member saying that he does not expect this bill to be a perfect bill. That is quite all right, as none of them are.
He then draws a parallel between the bill and the results which he expects from it and a new born child as compared with a man able to go out and do a day's work in the hayfield. He said that it requires development, the child must grow up. I want it understood that that is his illustration, not mine, but perhaps I may follow it up. Perhaps we might inquire into the origin of this baby. Possibly some beautiful daughter of Pharaoh, disguised as the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir)

I do not know a more complete disguise which she could assume-wandered down and found this marketing Moses in the bullrushes of Winnipeg North Centre. At least that is a charitable suggestion. If you do not accept that, then I am afraid that I must submit thaft this is an offspring of illicit relations between, shall we say, high reactionary influences, on the one hand, and thinly disguised communism, on the other. This is a hybrid offspring and those who have studied biology say that where the parents of an offspring are members of races entirely divergent, the offspring seldom makes a desirable citizen. He is apt to have the vices of both races and the virtues of neither. I should like to know w}io is going to assume responsibility for the suckling of this legislative foundling. Shall we have to wait until it grows up and see what is going to happen then? I suggest that the offspring had better be put in a lethal chamber and the parents sterilized to prevent any more such unfortunate accidents.
The hon. gentleman then states that in his opinion this bill offers some hope. He is a gentleman of ability with the facility of expressing himself. He was determined to find good in this bill but the best he can say of it is that it provides a hope. Have hon. mem-
[Mr. Neill.1
bers ever seen a man who has tried to live on hope? I did once and I must say that he was a sorry looking spectacle, be looked like a clothesline in an advanced stage of disintegration. I do not think I would like to live on hope and I should like to see this bill offer something more immediately profitable than hope.
I shall come back to the remarks of my hon. friend later on, but I would like to turn for a moment to the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), which appear on page 3689 of Hansard. I say with absolute sincerity that he is one of the finest speakers in his party. He is a man of almost nationwide reputation and possesses the facility of expressing himself and making the best out of any situation. I shall quote only a remark here and there as I have not time to do more. He says:
I am supporting this measure not because it is a particularly good one-there are many weakneses in it

And again he says:
I am in favour of the bill, but I still object to certain bureaucratic features which are embodied in section 9.
I thank him for those good words because they show that he realizes along with myself some of the obligations of section 9.
Then again:
It will be wasteful and will likely lead to a good deal of confusion and conflict later on.
Confusion and conflict in these matters means litigation, and while these things are being threshed out in the courts, the people who are trying to sell tomatoes will be waiting for a decision. Then in his closing remarks he says:
But we have to take what we can get under existing conditions; a slice of bread is better than no bread.
I suppose under some conditions that is true but if you have paid a high price for a loaf of bread, if the people have been told they are going to get a loaf of bread, is it not our duty, we who are informed, to point out that the public is not going to get the loaf of bread which has been dangled before them but is going to get only a slice? In the opinion of the hon. member for Bow River, a slice of bread is all that we are going to get. I hope we do get a slice but I have my doubts about that. If these were the remarks of some ordinary backbencher they might be considered as mere figures of speech,

Marketing Act-Mr. Neill
but it is a different thing when they are said by someone of the ability of the hon. member. He then concludes by saying:
For what merit it may have I am willing to accept the bill and shall vote for the third reading.
For what merit it "may" have, notice-may have-he will vote for the bill. Is that the best this bill offers us? I am not a bridge expert but I seem to remember having heard of a partner apologizing for what seemed like a dumb lead by saying, "I am sorry, partner, but I was leading out of weakness."

He was asked by the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) whether he thought this bill would bring about the result he hoped for, namely, to raise the price level of the product, say, of the wheat farmer. Assuming that the bill does all that we hope it will do; assuming that we succeed in the coming years in raising prices to a reasonable level-

He agrees with me. I ask any body of farmers, or any individual member from the prairies who speaks solely from the point of view of the wheat grower and who believes it would be better if wheat were left out of this bill, this question: Have you any right to come to British Columbia and insist that the people in the fish business, the people in the lumber business, the people in the sawmill business, in the shingle business, in reduction plants, in the dairying business, in paper manufacturing and so on, all of whom did not want to be brought under this bill, should be brought under the provisions of the bill? Have they the right to come to British Columbia or to any portion of the dominion and ask that? Is that not logical and is that not a fair question? Should they seek to force someone to take something for which they have not asked and which they do not want when they themselves are not willing to submit to it except as a last resort?
We have heard a good deal about the support which should be given to this bill, but I have not received any letters asking me to vote for the measure. I think much of this so-called support for the bill is due to ignorance of what it really means. Unfortunately we have got into the habit of believing in shibboleths, slogans and headlines. I suppose it is the present unrest and discontent that make us grasp at anything that comes along. We merely look at headlines, taking no time to read what is printed underneath, and so very often we do not know just what is contained under such headlines; we fail ,to get the meaning. I saw an article the other day in regard to a certain bill-I will not mention the bill; it was not this one at any rate. But under a large headline there was a statement something like this, "Commend Bennett" on a certain measure, and the article went on to say that that legislation had been warmly received by the Saskatchewan and Alberta premiers; that information appeared in smaller headlines. Now what does the man in the street say when he comes across something like that in the newspapers, when he sees that Premier Brownlee is reported as being in favour of certain legislation? That particular piece of legislation, I may say in passing, is all right; but the point is that all such large headlines, like the one to which I am referring-"Commend Bennett", and so on,-do not convey the precise facts. In this particular instance there
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

appears this statement at the bottom of the article, giving the views of Mr. Brownlee:
So far as I can judge from the press report, I am pleased with the legislation. Until I have had an opportunity of studying its actual working it will be impossible for me to pass a final opinion.
But what do the headlines say? "Glory to God in the highest; we are all for the bill; that is what we want." The man in the street says, in connection, with the bill now before us, "I am in favour of this measure; I am all for it." Of course; everybody wants it. But let us first see just what it means. The Minister of National Health has before the house a bill to prevent people from peddling cure-alls for certain fatal diseases like tuberculosis and cancer, without a doctor's prescription, because such a practice is said to be unfair; and a year or two ago he passed a bill to compel anyone selling quack remedies, or even genuine remedies, to put the formula on the bottle so that the purchaser would know, or would be able to have someone tell him, just what the contents were. Well, I wish the government would introduce something like that in connection with legislation, forbidding bills being described as cure-alls, making it compulsory to put the formula on the bottle, so to speak, so that people might know precisely what any particular measure meant, instead of having it dangled before their eyes as a cure-all, and being told that everybody is in favour of it.
I have here a letter from a friend to whom I sent a copy of this bill with a request for his opinion, and the pertinent part of the reply is this:
I have not had time to follow all the changes in the bill but it seems to me to be a step in the right direction. I would have liked to have seen it modelled closely on the British act.
I am afraid he will wait a long time to see it modelled on that act, because he does not realize what the bill really means. When he does-and I will make it my business to inform him-I doubt whether he will go even as far as he does in this letter.
As regards the amendment, I am glad to see it although I do not agree entirely with some of its conditions; but I should certainly like to see the bill referred back to the committee, and there is no reason why the government should not accept that suggestion, because it would not mean their defeat. If the bill were referred back to the committee it is possible that some of the amendments I have suggested would be considered.
As to how I shall vote, I am not ashamed of the vote I cast on the second reading, and

I hope not to be ashamed of my attitude towards the third reading. I believe in marketing control; we need it badly, first, for regulating quality of production going overseas, and secondly for regulating quantity. And if the minister had begun as the Minister of Justice suggested quite properly with respect to one of the proposed amendments, there would be no difficulty now. The Minister of Justice suggested in regard to that particular amendment that we should walk before we run, but here we are galloping. If we had begun with exports only there would have been no trouble in relation to jurisdiction to hamper us, and time would have shown us how the scheme worked out. It worked well in New Zealand and probably it would work well with us. But the control should be democratic. If you look at the introduction to the British act, 1931, you will find the statement that the bill is founded on the principle of democratic control. Does anyone suggest that that principle is found here? This bill allows control to pass into the hands of possibly a few marketers or people appointed by politicians, or by government-appointed boards. The scheme will be under the control of men not elected by the producers, not elected by anyone.
I refuse to be cowed by the threat that the people whom I represent want this bill and that I shall therefore find myself in disrepute if I vote against the third reading of it, as I will. Some of the people may have been stampeded with the idea of a cure-all as a marketing bill, but I have studied the measure day and night very carefully and have compared it with both the New Zealand bill and the British act, and surely there is not much wrong or unpatriotic or undemocratic in following the British and the New Zealand way. I cannot see that there is sufficient resemblance between those measures and the bill now before us to justify my voting for the third reading. I may be taking my political future in my hands in making this statement, but that is my duty, what I am sent for, what I am paid for. But, after studying the bill carefully, I am of the opinion that in the long run this bill will prove prejudicial to the producers of the country.

On the second reading I stated positively that unless the bill were amended substantially I would vote against the third reading. I have read carefully the amendments that have been proposed by the Minister of Agriculture <Mr. Weir) and most of the speeches made

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa
in committee, and I have no hesitation in concluding, as my deskmate has done, that I must vote against the third reading of this bill.
On the second reading I dwelt only upon two features of this piece of legislation: the constitution of the federal board and the basic principle upon which the local boards were to be established. I adhere to the idea that, *whether we like it or not, we must establish some machinery to control the exchange of trade between Canada and foreign countries. In this respect I cannot follow my good old friend from Ontario (Mr. Moore), though I enjoyed immensely the speech he made the other day to the tune of Old Liberalism. A policy of control is imposed upon us by circumstances as they exist the world over, and for that reason I voted for the second reading of the bill. The establishment of a federal board calling for the expenditure of public money could not be introduced in this house except as a government measure. Therefore, in common with other members of the house, I had no choice but to vote for or against *the second reading of the bill. But I then expressed my strong opposition to the manner in which it was proposed to constitute the local boards.
Amendments have been brought forward and accepted, the main one being the amendment which enables the government-not forces upon the government but enables the government-to call for a poll, that is, for a vote of the people concerned in each locality where such a local board will be proposed. I have already expressed the view, which I now repeat, that I am not a strong believer in the supreme wisdom of majorities any more than in that of minorities. My opposition to the composition of local boards is not based on the fact that they are either majority or minority boards. I am strongly convinced *that, given the conditions that exist in this country, geographical, ethnical and social, if we permit the creation of these small local units in every centre of each province of the dominion, we shall have chaos in matters of production and marketing and in all matters which are supposed to be adjusted by this legislation.
I have compared those local boards with the collective farms in Russia, the Kolkoczi. The more I have studied this legislation and compared it with the establishment of those organizations in Russia, the more I feel I am justified in calling this portion of the bill the sovietic part of it. The hon. member for
Regina (Mr. Turnbull), to whom I always listen with pleasure because he has the rare faculty of expressing his thoughts clearly and concisely, said that there was nothing socialistic in this legislation. In a sense that is true because there is nothing so antagonistic to modern socialism, as it is understood and practised in England or in Germany, as communism in Russia. As a matter of fact, after the communists in Russia did away with the old monarchical system, the first obstacle which they removed was that of the moderate socialists. I do not think there can be any doubt that the basic principle of this second part of the bill is that upon which those local bodies have been recognized in Russia. It is the acknowledgment, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, that the basis of social and economic conditions is no longer that of population or of community interest but of certain occupations. Tomato growers, poultry raisers, dairy producers form a small combine in a locality; they put up a scheme and they get approval in Ottawa. They immediately become masters of the production, indirectly if you like. I will admit that production is not mentioned here; but the minute they control the manner in which the product will be raised and put on the market, they really control production. What is the use of a man growing tomatoes if he is not allowed to sell them unless he puts himself under the iron-set regulations of the local board approved by the central board? Therefore the board indirectly controls production; it controls marketing and the disposition of the goods that will be produced in each locality controlled by a board. For that reason alone I am staunchly opposed to the bill as it stands. No amendment has been proposed and adapted by the committee to remove that obnoxious feature of the legislation. So much for that.
But the point I want to stress now is one which I left aside altogether on the second reading of this bill; I mean, the last portion of the legislation, clause 12. At least I call it the last portion because it comes before the investigation which is another piece of legislation in itself. As a matter of fact this is a combination of three bills in one. I refer to that clause upon which the leader of the opposition dwelt concerning restriction of imports and exports. I was rather surprised, not to hear because I was not present, but to read the observation made by my excellent young friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) with regard to this part of the bill. He said that those extraordinary powers

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa
which we are asked to grant to the governor in council enabling it to restrict at its will imports and exports of all the natural products as defined in this legislation-and the scope of natural products involved is very large-cannot be exercised unless upon recommendation by some local board or the federal board. It -may appear pretentious on my part to contradict the Solicitor General, who is a distinguished lawyer while I am not; the only title I have is that I am the dean of law students in Canada. I entered the study of law some forty years ago and I quitted it because, as old Paul Playdell said in one of Sir Walter Scott's novels, of the less honourable parts of the profession. Therefore I did not take my degree. But during my twenty-five years of parliamentary life I have acquired some habit of studying statutes. I remember a minister of justice who used to send me bills with this rather queer kind of compliment: " Bourassa, you are no lawyer; you know nothing about the law, but I have some reliance on your common sense and especially your aptitude to tell me what you think. Therefore I will consult you rather than any of my legal advisers." I thereby acquired the habit of construing statutes.
The first thing which strikes one with any experience of legislation is that clause 12 stands by itself without any connection whatever with the rest of the legislation. It reminds one of certain pieces of legislation introduced in the English parliament at a time the House of Lords still exercised its powers. When the Commons wanted the Lords to swallow a piece of legislation they did not like, they tacked it on to a money bill; and the House of Lords, not having power to amend money bills, were obliged to either swallow the whole thing or to reject it wholesale. This looks very much as if the government wanted to get from the house powers similar to those which President Roosevelt secured from congress, and they are trying to get them in this way instead of asking the house for the granting of those powers, a discussable, debatable question. I am not now so much enamoured-perhaps because I am older and the power of love may have decreased in me-as the leader of the opposition is of the goddess of parliamentary liberty. That goddess has been so unfaithful to her worshippers and lovers in the last twenty-five years that in my opinion we must show a little independence toward her; but at the same time I do not believe in deceit; I do not believe in roundabout ways. I may have admiration for a man like Mussolini taking his opponents by the throat, throwing them out of parliament and

telling them: "I do not want any opposition, because an opposition is an impediment to efficient government." That is his principle and, I repeat, it is a debatable one. In times of crises there is not the slightest doubt that a good autocrat is preferable to any debating house such as we are; and that many things such as the present Prime Minister has in mind would be better executed if he had no cabinet around him and no house of commons to discuss his views. But I repeat what I said three or four years ago: so long as we have a parliament and form part of it, we must at least have a certain degree of apparent respect for what we are supposed to represent. Being a member of this house I refuse to be stampeded into accepting, under the guise of legislation to regulate the marketing of products, a law which, without any reference to marketing, without any reference to the rights of the producers and consumers or to their interests, individual or collective, grants to the governor in council the power, in any manner, way, shape or form, to restrict the import or export of any natural product, such as it is defined by this legislation. It means a great deal-the foodstuffs derived from natural products, the products of the forests, the products of the fisheries, and so forth. Once this legislation is passed, the governor in council, with or without the advice of its central board, or of any local board, may decide one morning to close the door to the importation of Russian coal as it did, for what purpose I do not know, but the result was the commencement of the most damnable monopoly which now exists in the Dominion of Canada. It may order to-morrow the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) or the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) or anyone concerned in the lumbering trade, that he has no right to ship lumber to the United States; that in order to favour imperial policies he must sell it in London at whatever price he can get. All that can be done by order in council under clause 12 without any reference to the opinion of any local board or of the central board. How could my good friend the Solicitor General say that those powers cannot be exercised unless upon the advice of a board? Clause 12 is quite clear; it states:
The governor in council may by order or regulation, notice whereof shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette-
(a)	regulate or restrict the importation into Canada of any natural product which enters Canada in competition with a regulated product;
(b)	regulate or restrict the exportation from Canada of any natural product;

Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa
And so on. I refer only to those two subclauses. What is the title of this bill?
An act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith.
That does not contain the slightest indication that there will be any restriction on imports and exports. In all the clauses dealing with the composition of the federal and local boards and the powers assigned to them there is not the slightest indication with regard to imports. Then, under one single clause which stands by itself, granting extraordinary powers to the governor in council without relation to the rest of the law, to the powers of the central board or the requests of the local boards, the governor in council is authorized to do whatever it likes in matters of import and export. It may establish new tariffs. It may suppress certain commodities. It may establish quotas. To-morrow it may tell the apple growers of Nova Scotia:	"This year
you will not send a barrel of apples to England, because we want to favour British Columbia." It may tell the eheesemakers of Quebec that Ontario must have a chance, and that no Quebec cheese may be sent to England until Ontario has disposed of its product. I do not say it will do that sort of thing, but I say this legislation authorizes the governor in council to do anything it pleases, either by way of tariffs or by most arbitrary restrictions with regard to imports and exports. It may upset the whole trade of the country without any indication of the will of parliament or the desire or interest of the people for whose benefit this legislation is supposed to be adopted.
