I leave that aside. I want to impress those who take the trouble to read my few remarks with the bearing of this one clause.
Now connect this with the extraordinary powers we have granted the government under the guise of peace, order and good government. Take those two laws together, and if thereby and thereunder you have not the amplest form of fascism that can exist, I want to know where it can be found.
In this bill you have this extraordinary feature of a moderate form of state socialism in the first part, which I think is a necessity. You have a disguised form of sovietism in the second part, and you have a most striking form of fascism in the third part. That is 74726-23S
too much for me to swallow at once. I can stand a good deal. I have been taken to task by some virtuous people in my province for having expressed myself as prepared to stand a good deal of socialism, not as a doctrine but as a necessity. For example, I stand the extremely socialist law enacted by the Quebec government in the matter of sale of liquor. That is state socialism, pure and simple. I have submitted under protest to the so-called assistance law of the Quebec government, which is socialized charity. I do not approve of that, but we have it. I am amused when my good liberal friends stand so strongly against socialism here, though they go through the rural districts of Quebec praising Mr. Taschereau and his government for their kindness to the poor since they adopted the most socialistic law with regard to the sustenance of charitable institutions. So, as I say, I am prepared to stand a good deal but I am not prepared to stand sovietism in any shape or form. That is what I denounced on the second reading; that is what I still denounce. No remedy has been proposed; nothing has been done to correct it. I denounce it not only because of the obnoxious principle at the base of that portion of the law; I denounce it in the interests of the small people, the small producers and especially the consumers.
In that regard I agree entirely with the right lion, leader of the opposition, and I support his amendment which states that nothing has been done and something should be done to protect the consumer. I am also concerned about the fate of the numerous producers who will be dominated by these local boards whether, as I repeat for the third or fourth time, they are majority or minority boards; that does not concern me for the present. I am concerned about the liberty of action of the producers in the cultivation of their land for the production of whatever they think it can produce, which they know far better than any board in Ottawa or even any local board can know. I object to any group of individuals engaged in raising poultry or in producing tomatoes or potatoes imposing their manner of cultivation and their system of production upon people who may have good reason for producing something else in a different way
My reason for supporting the second reading of this bill was my feeling that a body should be created to direct the economic activities of our farmers, to make them understand that if they produce too much of one commodity the price will fall, and that they should produce something else or some other quality of fruit, of vegetables or of



Marketing Act-Mr. Bourassa
live stock. But I object to a local board more than I object to a federal board imposing its ways upon its neighbours or upon any minority in any locality. We must tell the whole truth. In this country there is less social spirit and public spirit than in the old countries, where traditions have been established, where for years people have been forced, so to speak, to be considerate of each other. In all new countries, but especially in the United States and 'Canada, the prevailing law of economics is the law of selfishness, the law of getting all the money you can by any means you can. The moment you permit small groups of individuals all through the land to impose their views, to protect their selfish interests, they will impose them in such a way that not only will they antagonize the minority; not only will they impose upon the public sacrifices which they find hard enough to make to-day in being forced to pay twice as much as they should for what they buy; at the same time this will upset the economic life of this country under the pretence of organizing it.
The Minister of Agriculture is a right thinking man; I believe he wants to do the right thing, but I am afraid he has listened to too much advice of various kinds. In times of trouble and crisis all sorts of quack doctors rise up, in universities, in farm districts and in labour organizations. Each has his own remedy, and they come to the government. When governments give way and take a little of the medicine of each they are apt to compound a mixture that will poison the whole body, politic and social. It would have been better to start humbly; but unfortunately, as one great French writer has said, we have lost the sense of the great political virtue of humility. Every one imagines he is bound to be a big man, to produce big things all of a sudden, with a big piece of law which will cure all. I am afraid that is the wrong way. For a number of years we have been going down hill. For at least twenty-five years back we have gone crazy,-and in that statement I do not except myself, because, as an old friend of mine, a specialist in mental diseases, once said to me, "You know, we have certain theories; we put a certain number of people in asylums 'because we believe they are suffering from this or that kind of mental disease, but, to be perfectly truthful I believe everyone is crazy; it is only a question of degree and manner. I know that every day in business and social circles I meet people who are far more crazy than those people in the asylum of which I am superintendent."

I am afraid that for the last twenty-five years, and especially in economic methods, we have all gone crazy. We have built up everything on credit, indebtedness, extravagance, legislation,-laws, laws, laws, laws- without reflection before they have been passed, without seriousness when they are applied, and without any moral sanction to get the people to agree to their application. What is the use of passing laws which are inapplicable? I am sure the Minister of Agriculture, and I am still more sure-because I know him better-the Prime Minister knows that this law cannot be applied as it is. He knows that if it were applied as it is, or rather if in its application there was an endeavour to meet all the requirements and exigencies of the people who have asked for it, it would simply upset the whole economic life of this country. It would raise community against community, class against class, country against city, and advance the progress of social or economic revolution far more than the extremest revolutionary party could do; they would do it by bad legislation and by improper administration.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I vote heartily for the amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition, and still more heartily against the third reading, of the bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that the debate upon this measure should have taken a very considerable length of time is not surprising. That it should have generated some heat without much light is somewhat amazing, and that it should have wandered over many fields of discussion is not strange for the motion now before the house is for the third reading of the so called marketing bill.

speechtext: So called!

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
It is somewhat interesting to realize that it was so called by the hon. gentlemen opposite yesterday. Their recognition of its real value is something that should not pass without comment.

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
I think perhaps the most interesting thing that has developed during the debate of yesterday and to-day and the day before is the difference of opinion between those who united unsuccessfully to vote for the amendment that has just been negatived.
The veteran former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has expressed himself in that firm and determined manner that has characterized his life's conduct in matters political. He has always had strong convictions and expressed them with a fervour and determination worthy of his race. I have heard him cheered and cheered and cheered by hon. gentlemen opposite, but there was a rare silence yesterday when he was concluding his observations. Whether or not that marked his colleagues' disapproval of his observations I cannot say.
Then there was the member for Quebec East, the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). When you compare his attitude towards this bill with that of many other members who have spoken from his side, you have a very great cleavage of opinion. Then when you compare the speech of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) with that of some of those who have spoken you begin to realize that after all there still remains in this house some vestige of the opinion that was held during the early Victorian days.
The Iaissez faire doctrines have not disappeared entirely. There are those who believe that the only way in which progress can be made is to watch the procession pass by but there are also those who believe that changed times and changed conditions must be met with new policies. Fortunately, the Conservative party belongs to the latter class.

speechtext: That is new.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I should judge that in the mind of the hon. gentleman anything would be new. The fact is that we still believe in the truth of that statement made by Tennyson:
That man's the true Conservative
Who lops the moulder'd branch away.
We offer no apology for standing where we do with respect to a matter of this kind. I was somewhat amazed in following the very excellent historical review made yesterday by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), when he was dealing with certain phases of economic history, that he should not have observed that we have here in these days-I remind the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore)-a situation not unlike that which prevailed in England in the early days of Queen Victoria's reign, in fact up until
the middle of the nineteenth century. The Iaissez faire doctrine developed to a point never before reached. It was declared that contracts were sacred and that governments must not interfere with business, that the father could rent the services of his child at the age of six and that he should work until he was twelve. We find factories where girls and boys of five, six, seven, eight and nine years of age were working.
If those who are interested will take the trouble to look up the Register for 1847 they will find the history of that bill which was introduced in the English House of Commons by Mr. Fielden and supported by Lord Ashley, afterwards Lord Shaftesbury. They will then realize the extent to which under the development of that doctrine business could not be touched by legislation. They will see the extent to which child labour was exploited, that contracts must be maintained and there should be no interference or regulation of the business world. If hon. members of this house are interested they can look this up as I shall not take the time this afternoon to read the rather interesting developments of that doctrine. One must not change the hours of labour from the twelve hours contracted for alike by father and child. They will find how the suggestion that these hours should be reduced to eleven hours per day met with disapproval. They will find how the suggestion that they should be reduced to ten hours met with strong opposition on the ground that it would reduce the productive power of the factories by twenty-five per cent. These things are matters of history.
There were those who felt that the Iaissez faire doctrine had been carried to extremes in the early part of the nineteenth century. Mr. Fielden from Lancashire compared the death rate of children between one and ten years in Manchester with those in London. Just why there has been interference with that doctrine was admirably presented yesterday by the hon. member for Ontario. We can realize that interference by legislatures and by parliaments has been in the interests of the state itself, its people, its population and the lives of the people. Interference has been against child labour, against long hours of labour. The endeavour has been to secure conditions for those who labour which will enable them to have at least a little leisure. Within my memory there stood in this house an hon. gentleman who came from the old county of Northumberland in England and who recalled the times of the election of John Morley in Newcastle.
Morley declared that any interference with the hours of labour was contrary to the
3762	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
doctrine of his party, that laissez faire meant that there should be no interference by the state with respect to contractual obligations entered into by citizens. That is the doctrine which is preached to-day in this house. It is the doctrine which was preached yesterday by the hon. member for Ontario but neither he nor the leader of the opposition dared say in this house that he did not believe the state should interfere in the regulation of business with respect to hours of labour, with respect to factory conditions, with respect to child labour and with respect to health and sanitation. Certainly, business must be interfered with and regulated, there must be interference by the state on behalf of those who unless they can speak collectively cannot care for themselves.
We now have the application to agriculture of that same principle which they dare not disapprove and those who are unable to organize themselves even as the trade unions have organized in Great Britain. When such legislation is presented, we are told that it is despotic and that it means tyrannical interference with the rights of the people of this country to do as they please. There is a time in the history of every country when voices have arisen. Let me remind this house of the circumstances under which the state in Great Britain regulated the hours of labour and so on. It will be recalled that Mr. Fielden, a distinguished manufacturer from Lancashire, and Lord Ashley found it difficult to interest the great masses of the people who had been brought up on the doctrine of laissez faire to take any action with respect to these matters. Year in and year out Samuel Plimsoll demanded that the load mark should be placed upon ships but he met with powerful opposition from the shipowners. But he was persistent and insistent and in the end every ship that leaves an English port must bear upon her side the Plimsoll mark, an eternal memorial to the persistency of one man for his cause. Because of the impotency of individuals and their inability to bring about the reforms they desired, we finally had the creation of the great trade unions in Great Britain. Who were their opponents? The exponents of laissez-faire. Their opponents said: We will not tolerate this, these institutions must not be permitted to say how contracts shall be made, what the hours of labour shall be and what shall be the conditions under which men and women work. But the trade unions triumphed. Why? Because the rights of humanity prevailed over the rights of dividends. In the ultimate analysis that will be found to be the real reason and nothing else.

Can agriculture organize? Yesterday and to-day the veteran former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) gave the long story of the efforts of agriculture towards organization. He told the story of the granges and the patrons of industry, he told of the struggles for organization on the part of agriculture and of the failures brought about by certain circumstances. I realize that their position is not that of the trade unionists. They have not the voice which the trade unions have to make themselves effective in the constituencies in order that laissez faire may not prevail against them. The time has come when the natural products of this country shall be marketed under conditions which will ensure to those who produce them some measure of return for their efforts, a measure of return relative to that which the trade unions have been able to secure by organization for those whom they represent.
There you have the analogy. If any of you desire to take the trouble to read carefully the economic history of the period to which I have referred you will find the continued opposition that was made against this combination of effort, this desire to organize for the purpose I have mentioned. If any of you are interested, I suggest that you take the trouble to secure in yonder library one of these volumes and read it. To-day you have the parallel in this house. All those who have consistently followed the doctrine of laissez faire, as the right hon. gentleman opposite, the hon. member for Ontario, and others do, are banded together against this legislation. Just as in the days of the trade union effort all those who held that property rights and the rights of contract must be supreme over every other consideration in the world, were banded together for that purpose, so to-day, to the left of the Speaker, with one or two exceptions we find banded together those who say, "Let well enough alone. Let there be no interference with business or with the right of contract; let there be no interference to improve the conditions under which the farmer shall market his products; let there be no interference by the state, by legislation, to ensure for him a larger part of the consumer's dollar; let us blind the issue by talking about the rights of consumers, about the constitutional history of the past; let us call up Magna Charta so that we may remember what John did at Bunnymede, let us concern ourselves with all these things, but let us ensure that the end sought here shall not be attained."

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
That is the story. It is just as it was in the middle of the nineteenth century-the sacred rights of contract and of property, the sacred rights of those who must be permitted to maintain the foreign trade of England. I was reading the other day one of the speeches of this sort insisting upon the maintenance of that condition at any cost. Was it to cut down the hours of labour? No, but to maintain foreign trade. To improve the condition of the agrarian, to assist him in marketing his products, to provide for a cooperative effort on the part of local communities, created by themselves, and assisted by the state? No; that must not be. Let us maintain the doctrines of the past-that is the attitude. Let us remember the sacred name of Morley, nor let us forget Hume; so that by and by, if we are long enough at it, we shall drift back to the days of the barons at Runnymede.
Now I do challenge one observation among others made by the right hon. gentleman yesterday. He asserted that the world is the same to-day as it was in days gone by; that there is nothing new under the sun; that the great conflict of the ages has made no great structural change; but that, if you look at the end of the reign of George IV, you will find a fitting similarity to the conditions that exist to-day.
I have too much respect for the intellectual powers of the right hon. gentleman to believe for a single moment that he had given any thought to that statement before he made it. Just think of the conditions through which the world has passed. Why is it that the world will never again be as it was before 1914? Not the youngest man in this house, not the youngest page here will ever see a return to the conditions that existed before 1914. Why? It is so obvious that it is hardly necessary to state the reason. First of all, not merely thousands and hundreds of thousands but millions of the finest lives in all the world have gone out for the cause of war, not in one part of the world but practically in every part. Secondly, on the purely material side, the debts that have been incurred on so vast a scale were incurred not for the construction of productive and useful undertakings but in the destruction of the very things which were bought with the money that paid for them. In cotton, in powder, in explosives, in everything that goes to the maintenance of war, millions and hundreds of millions, nay, thousands of millions were destroyed, and as a result there was no productive return for the money thus expended. But it did not end there. At
the close of the war there was this condition -and I commend the thought to this house.
The figures produced by the Secretary of Agriculture for the United States indicate that at the end of the war the combatant nations had reduced by fifty million acres the land which they had had under cultivation -fifty million acres. WThy? Because, unlike the Napoleonic wars, unlike the wars in which the armies of Wellington and of Marlborough participated, the belligerents did not look to the communities through which they passed to provide them with food. The food came from overseas, from remote parts of the world. Transports were carrying food, meat, flour, grain, from the remotest parts of the world during the war, and what happened? Fifty million acres of land, in the warring countries, went out' of cultivation. In the United States alone, forty million acres were put under cultivation during the war-forty million acres that had not previously been cultivated-to meet the wants of those who were warring, and who had abandoned fifty million acres of farm land. And what was the position in Canada? Between the outbreak of the war and the end there were put under cultivation in this country over twenty million more acres. The result was that there were over sixty million additional acres under cultivation in Canada and the United States between the outbreak of hostilities and the end and shortly thereafter, to provide food, to provide the various requirements of the people who had abandoned lands because compulsory service had made it necessary for them to fight.
With peace, what happened? With peace there was an effort to bring back a return of pre-war conditions. Those who survived went back to their farms and endeavoured to till the soil and to produce. In this country we did not at once abandon the increased acreage but continued to maintain it, as they did in the United States, and in the end there occurred what was inevitable. To the extent to which those who had abandoned their farms to engage in the conflict went back and brought those farms once more into production, to that extent they were supplying wants that had been supplied by Canada and the United States, and this rendered it impossible for those engaged in similar occupations in Canada and the United States to find a market for their products.
Does anyone suggest that such a situation has ever existed in the world before? What brought it about? Compare the end of George's reign with what happened at the close of the last war. At the end of George's reign steam as a motive power was unknown;

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
electricity was not heard of for commercial purposes; the internal combustion engine was yet a dream in the mind of an inventor not yet born. That is the position. All these changes came into being, and you can no more compare the conditions that existed at the end of George's reign with the conditions that existed at the close of the last war than you can compare the conditions, of which we have any record at all, that existed in the glacial age with present conditions.
Under these circumstances, what is the duty and function of government?

speechtext:
It may be a joke to
some hon. gentlemen but there are agriculturists who do not think it a joke. It well might be that the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson), who is so agitated by the loss of a market by importation of flour from abroad, will treat it as a joke. But the people concerned do not so regard it.
Let us see what the position was. I have indicated in a few sentences the effect so far as agriculture is concerned. With respect to industry, what is the situation? The hon. member for Ontario yesterday briefly touched upon it. There was an abandonment also of all industrial activities except those that were related to war. Coal was produced so that T.N.T. might be supplied; cotton was produced so that there might be high explosives and so on right down, and the factories, the industrial life of the communities that were at war, were engaged in the manner I have indicated, the industries being developed to the highest point of production for war purposes, for instance, chemical gases and commodities of that sort.
At the end of the war the readjustment period began. As I have dealt with this once in the house I shall not repeat. The readjustment period with respect to industry we passed through, but as regards agriculture the condition was far different; there is no condition comparable with it. Here were men upon the farms that they had created for the purpose of supplying the deficits in food in the warring countries, and the warring countries were now supplying their own food by the toil of the men who had left the colours for the purpose of going back to their farms; that was the situation. Under those circumstances, what have governments done? The other day I pointed out in the house that France had taken immediate action for two reasons: she did not desire to pay $3 or S2.50

for wheat; she did not desire to be held up, as she regarded it, to ransom as long as she could cultivate her soil and supply her cereal wants. In addition to that she was not prepared to take the risk, if once more engaged in war, of the destruction of wheat transports by submarines and other methods such as torpedoes and mines. What did she do? Someone has referred to her policy as one of intense nationalism. What she did was to declare that she proposed to the extent of the ability of her people to make herself in food self-sustaining. In Italy, Germany and other European countries similar conditions prevailed and to the exent that they prevailed, there was a lessening of the markets which had been created for us by reason of 'the war in those countries during the war.
Faced with that condition here we have Canada in which about half the population is engaged in tilling the soil, and there again the right hon. gentleman and I would disagree. At the end of the reign of George IV you had the agricultural population, the yeoman of England, the country squires, the parliament that was one of landed interests only and you had in addition a certain measure of, shall I say, cooperative harmony in Great Britain between those who tilled the soil and those who owned it. In this country the major part of the population for many years after confederation was on the soil; it tilled the soil; but the great mechanization of the world that took place through the inventive genius of man affecting the whole attitude of mankind toward production in agriculture, sent into the cities and towns great masses of the people and left on the countryside smaller and smaller numbers of them. In a most interesting book written recently, Mr. A. G. Street, who came out to western Canada and lived in Manitoba, points out the great differences that have arisen in England in connection with that matter during the last fifty years. The countryside was once dotted with thriving farms. Now you have black chimneys and factories everywhere. That condition to a similar extent exists in Canada. For the first time the last census indicates that in this country more than one-half of the population is in the cities and towns, leaving less than one-half of the papulation inhabiting the farms and working and tilling the soil.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
After Recess

Mr. Speaker, when the
house rose at six o'clock 1 had concluded pointing out some of the reasons why, in my opinion, the extraordinary change of conditions which had been brought about by the great war necessitated legislative action being taken at least to afford to the agriculturists the same opportunity that was afforded to those who, in some ways, had been perhaps more fortunate in their association with industry.
I was much taken with the provisions made by various countries when they came to deal with the marketing of products, with the surplus of agricultural production as well as of industrial production. Each community and nation endeavoured to supply itself with its material wants, and most of them enacted some form of legislation providing for the marketing of their products in an orderly and planned manner. Perhaps among the nations that dealt last with the problem was Japan, and I was much taken with the English translation of a few words in the Japanese act: A law concerning the adjustment of trade and the safeguarding of commerce.
It was promulgated on April 7 and became effective as from May 1, 1934, and these words are worthy of consideration by this parliament. The spokesman of the foreign office said:
Promulgation of this law has been made necessary because there is a growing tendency in other countries to ignore the fundamental economic principle of ministering to one another's wants and promoting through their cooperative efforts the progress and prosperity of mankind-all of which are being reflected in their attempts to suppress importation of foreign goods by means of high tariffs, restriction of imports, etc., and particularly because there seems to be an increasing number of countries which are setting up barriers against Japan's export trade.
He concludes with these words:
Of course, Japan has no intention to take any step that is likely to increase the present difficulties of the world. Rather, she hopes there will be no occasion requiring an actual operation of this law.
The empire of Japan, in dealing with the problems incident to the conditions to which I have referred, enacted the law I have just mentioned. We in this country, finding ourselves confronted with like conditions, world conditions over which we had no control and which were not within our jurisdiction to control, had to take some action to avoid the possibility of absolute destruction. It is not
as though this were a new principle so far as the provinces are concerned. I do not think there are many provinces in this confederation-there may be a few-in which an effort has not been made, aided by the legislature, to enable the agriculturist to market his products under more satisfactory terms and conditions than are involved in merely sending them to market without regard to conditions. British Columbia has had a marketing act for many years.
I saw the wheat pool founded in Alberta, when Mr. Aaron Sapiro came to Calgary and, after meeting with those interested in the production of grain, finally induced them to believe that this would be a useful thing to do. They drew up an agreement, which was subsequently ratified by the legislature, and in my professional capacity I was asked to advise upon it, so I saw the foundation of the movement. I still think that no wheat pool has been operated more reasonably and more beneficially with regard to the people concerned than the pool in Alberta. Pools were formed also in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba. It well may be that when, without adequate experience, they endeavoured to project their idea into the world market without, as I say, having a full understanding of what was involved, they met with a measure of disaster, but that does not in any sense militate against the soundness of what they were endeavouring to do. They were opposed by the great interests; they were opposed by many others, but they maintained their position, and I heard the foremost banker of that time in Canada say that it had done more to enable the western farmer to care for his obligations and deal with his economic life in an orderly manner than any other single thing to which reference could be made.
The ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has referred to the efforts that were made in the eastern provinces. For constitutional reasons, at every turn and in every instance there was, of course, a limitation imposed upon their powers. No province could create a pool or make provision for cooperative marketing that gave jurisdiction or power beyond the territorial limits of the province in question. Questions of contracts and sales and matters of that kind were dealt with as property and civil rights, but when you went beyond the boundaries of the province and had to deal with communities beyond those boundaries, whether inter-provincially or internationally, of course you were subject to the play of forces which were not under the control of provincial legislatures.

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
Hence it was that they sought and, in some instances, by arrangement between themselves, exercised jurisdiction and power which otherwise they could not have obtained except by agreement with the dominion.
With that set of facts before us; with the economic conditions prevailing that I have mentioned; with the efforts and experiments in British Columbia with respect to fruit, apples, milk, potatoes and so on, what were we to do? I noticed in the press to-day that they allege that $300,000 has been lost to the growers of potatoes because this act could not be put in force in the province of British Columbia by reason of the delays that have occurred. In British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and some of the eastern provinces, within the limits imposed by the constitution, pools, or, if you like, associations or organizations having for their purpose the grouping together of individuals for the purpose of selling their products, have been in operation for years. But when the economic conditions that now prevail in this world are faced and you have to consider how you can best serve the interests of at least one-half of our population, and far more than half if you consider the production of new wealth from year to year, how is it to be dealt with?
I have been vastly amused and interested to observe the operation of the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. First there was complete and absolute opposition to a marketing bill. Then followed a long, protracted struggle in which some of the less prominent supporters asserted that their suggestions had been accepted as amendments and that the bill offered for third reading was not the bill offered for second reading. But alas and alack; think of what has happened. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has deprived his followers of the opportunity of saying that they have made a new bill, for he has now pronounced his opposition to the bill which emerged from the committee with the amendments attached. So the principle of the marketing bill, apposed as it was on the second reading, is now to be opposed, we are told, on the third reading. In view of my knowledge of the political history of this country in 1925 and 1926 I never expected to hear any ex-minister, who was so dependent at that time on the support of those who sat to the left, refer to those hon. members as "those birds". But I suspect that in using that term the hon. gentleman had [Mr. Bennett.l
regard to the fact that they have flown; I suspect that this was the real reason for that remark. And if of course they have flown, as in fact they have, the reasons for so doing-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says, to his sorrow, that they were migratory birds. They may have been in fact just that. But at any rate I think it was not quite the just deserts due to those who sit to the left that those who for many years had sat in high places with all the emoluments of power and honours of office, who enacted legislation for standardizing hay, straw and potatoes and several matters of that kind, but left dead upon the order paper many standardizing measures which would have been passed had the birds not flown, should thus refer to them in this debate.
This government, when confronted with the circumstances to which I have referred, had no doubts in the world that the only measure which could possibly be enacted by this parliament was one which would give force, validity and life to the efforts made by organizations within the provinces and created under their authority to function beyond the immediate boundaries of those provinces. Could anything else be more simple than that? That is the basis of it.
One hon. gentleman has said that this is socialism. If it is, he has been a party to it for a long time. If it is socialism, then 1 plead guilty to having been a supporter of it for many long years. I cannot think that there is anything offensive in calling it socialism, if you like, if you mean that the force and power of the parliament of Canada is to be utilized to enable those who live within provincial boundaries and have organized themselves into units to promote their material efforts, and to get something for the toil they give. You may call it anything you like, but at least it is sound legislation which promotes it.
\ ou thus have the local units organized and functioning. Then, you have your federal unit not for a rendezvous, as the exMinister of Agriculture has said, but as a great clearing house centre for the purposes of enabling those who by reason of limitations imposed upon them constitutionally are not familiar with international conditions to be able to deal in the light of the knowledge that is given them of the whole international situation. That is the central board. It is not only to be a disseminator of information;

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
it supplies the local units with such information as will enable them to determine how best to dispose of their products.
Why are you opposed to that? Why are those to the left of you, Mr. Speaker, rising in their places to-night and voting against a bill which provides for that? Have they given, in this long debate, any substitute for that which has been offered here? Have they offered a substitute? Has there been a single word of constructive criticism with respect to this measure? True, they did suggest some amendments-the crossing of a "t" and the dotting of an "i." They did suggest some amendments of that sort. Rightly it may be stated that they did suggest two or three. Every member has a duty to perform; he owes a duty to a measure before the house and if his suggestion is accepted by the government of the day, so much the better for the bill. Every hon. member must play a constructive part in it, to improve it, to make it better.
I do say that this legislation which was offered on the second reading of the bill which has now passed the committee and is submitted to the house for third reading-I say that this legislation embodies the idea that the central authority is to be utilized, with all its authority and with all its strength, with all its life and vitality, to enable the agrarian in the provinces, with the aid of his organizations, to have that knowledge which will enable him to deal with his calling, and to receive the best return for his effort. That is what we are endeavouring to do.

The hon. gentleman has
said that it is to deprive the minority of their right. His seat in this house deprives the minority of their rights. That is the basis of this type of government, if the hon. gentleman has any appreciation at all of what democratic representative institutions mean. They mean this, that the majority governs. How do we pass measures in this building? How do we do it? By the will of the majority. How do we do anything else? By the will of the majority. Representative institutions, involving the majority selecting their representatives, deprives minorities of their rights. That is the theory of our government, and as I said every hon. member who occupies a seat in this house is here, despite the opposition of a minority. And when that minority is converted into a majority. usually much to the chagrin of the person affected, then the will of that majority must prevail. That is the position.
We speak of liberty. "Oh liberty, what crimes have been committed in thy name!' No wonder that a great annotator referred to liberty in that way. Liberty-yes, there is no liberty that does not involve curtailment of rights.

When you talk about liberty, is there an hon. member in this house who does not realize that liberty means restraint, that liberty means discipline, that liberty means loss of unrestricted freedom? Why is it that you have by-laws in this city? Why do you make laws in the legislatures? Why do we pass laws in the dominion parliament? Why have we a criminal code? Why have we any of these provisions which say to the individual, "You may not exercise all your liberties"? Why? Because the enjoyment of any liberty, any constitutional liberty, means sacrifice by each individual of some of his natural liberties. And when a legislature takes from this class or that class, from this individual or that individual, some of his natural liberties, it speaks in the name of society and in the name of the state, in order that there may be an enjoyment of liberty by everyone within the realm. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Yes, in days gone by, but I commend the hon. gentleman to a consideration of this fact, that this is not a new doctrine. Fifty-one years ago a statute was passed by a celebrated Liberal government in Ontario of that day, the government of Sir Oliver Mowat. They passed a liquor licence act, and the question as to its validity went to the privy council. That was in 1883, just fifty-one years ago, and fifty-one years ago the argument made here now by the right hon. leader of the opposition and so heartily applauded by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) as soon as he saw how others were applauding, was made in that case. I wonder if this chamber has any realization of just how far the courts went with respect to that. The court held that:
"The Liquor License Act of 1877, c. 181, revised statutes of Ontario," which in respect of sections 4 and 5, makes regulations in the nature of police or municipal regulations of a merely local character for the good government of taverns, et cetera, does not in respect of those sections interfere with "the general regulation of trade or commerce," but comes within Nos. 8, 15 and 16 of section 92 of the act of 1867, and is within the powers of the provincial legislature.
Held, further, that the local legislature had power by the said act of 1867 to entrust to a board of commissioners authority to enact regulations of the above character, and thereby to create offences and annex penalties thereto.
"Imprisonment" in No. 15 of section 92 of the act of 1867 means imprisonment with or without hard labour.
That case is Hodge and the Queen. In that case the privy council laid down the rule that it was competent for the legislature of Ontario to create a body and give that body the power to licence, and to create criminal offences and fix punishments for those violating the law. That was not the legislature, but the licensing body that was set up by the legislature, and the argument made in this house the other day, with all the startling assertions I heard yesterday as to this being a modem doctrine, was made in the privy council when the case was heard by that body in 1883. Here are the words of the court in giving judgment with respect to that matter, and it does seem to me that they are very pertinent. The case was argued at great length. Mr. Kerr, Q.C., and Mr. Jeune, afterwards president of the probate division in England and afterwards Lord St. Hillier, argued the case for the appellant, and after the case had been heard at great length finally 
the court laid down this rule, a rule which I commend to the consideration of this house because it does appear to me that there has been an entire misapprehension as to the true construction to be placed on both the powers of parliament and the powers of the legislatures. Here are the words of the court in giving judgment:
Their lordships consider that the powers intended to be conferred by the act in question, when properly understood, are to make regulations in the nature of police or municipal regulations of a merely local character for the good government of taverns, et cetera, licensed for the sale of liquors by retail, and such as are calculated to preserve, in the municipality, peace and public decency, and repress drunkenness and disorderly and riotous conduct. As such they cannot be said to interfere with the general regulation of trade and commerce which belongs to the dominion parliament, and do not conflict with the provisions of the Canada Temperance Act, which does not appear to have as yet been locally adopted.
Then they proceeded:
Assuming that the local legislature had power to legislate to the full extent of the resolutions passed by the licence commissioners, and to have enforced the observance of their enactments by penalties and imprisonment with or without hard labour, it was further contended that the imperial parliament had conferred no authority on the local legislature to delegate those powers to the licence commissioners, or any other persons. In other words, that the power conferred by the imperial parliament on the local legislature should be exercised in full by that body, -and by that body alone.
We have heard that for the last ten days. The judgment continued:
It appears to their lordships, however, that the objection thus raised by the appellants is founded on an entire misconception of the true character and position of the provincial legislatures. They are in no sense delegates of or acting under any mandate from the imperial parliament. When the British North America Act enacted that there should be a legislature for Ontario, and that its legislative assembly should have exclusive authority to make laws for the province and for provincial purposes in relation to the matters enumerated in section 92, it conferred powers not in any sense to be exercised by delegation from or as agents of the imperial parliament, but authority as plenary and as ample within the limits prescribed by section 92 as the imperial parliament in the plenitude of its power possessed and could bestow. Within these limits of subjects and area the local legislature is supreme, and has the same authority as the imperial parliament, or the parliament of the dominion would have had under like circumstances to confide to a municipal institution or body of its own creation authority to make by-laws or resolutions as to subjects specified in the enactment, and with the object of carrying the enactment into operation and effect.
It is obvious-

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
And I commend these words to this chamber:
-that such an authority is ancillary to legislation and without it an attempt to provide for varying details and machinery to carry them out might become oppressive, or absolutely fail.
I heard the right hon. gentleman yesterday ask: Why is not the scheme before parliament? Why are not the details of the scheme here for us to pass upon? Well, the scheme will be arranged and promulgated after parliament has risen. Next year when parliament has met, it would deal with it. But what would be its value? What would be its value, I ask? The delegation of power, as I shall presently point out, is the basis of all constitutional legislation. Their lordships in delivering their judgment said:
An attempt to provide for varying details and machinery to carry them out might become oppressive, or absolutely fail.
The very full and very elaborate judgment of the court of appeal contains abundance of precedents for this legislation, entrusting a limited discretionary authority to others, and has many illustrations of its necessity and convenience. It was argued at the bar that a legislature committing important regulations to agents or delegates effaces itself.
Has this chamber ever heard that argument?

speechtext:
That is not so.
I am quoting now from the judgment:
It retains its powers intact, and can, whenever it pleases, destroy the agency it has created and set up another, or take the matter directly into its own hands.
There is the answer.
How far it shall seek the aid of subordinate agencies, and how long it shall continue them, arc matters for each legislature, and not for courts of law, to decide.
Fifty-one years ago the court of last resort in this empire made that statement of the law. It has been acted on ever since, and, as I shall presently indicate, by no one more than the right hon. gentleman himself. The judgment continues:
Their lordships do not think it necessary to pursue this subject further, save to add that, if by-laws or resolutions are warranted, power to enforce them seems necessary and equally lawful. Their lordships have now disposed of the real questions in the cause.
There was a later case from Australia which touched on parliament exercising jurisdiction in the same sense as this, the case of Powell against Apollo Candle Company. In that case discretion was given to a collector of customs
to determine what the tariff should be if there was no tariff on a particular commodity. If he thought it approximated in quality to some other commodity he might apply the duty on the commodity in question as he thought desirable. The statute is set out at length, and the case was decided in 1885, a little later than the case to which I have just referred. Even though it takes a few minutes to do it, in order that there may be no misunderstanding with respect to this fundamental principle, I am going to quote from the section which the privy council had to deal with:
Whenever any article of merchandise-
This was in the Customs Act:
-then unknown to the collector is imported, which, in the opinion of the collector or the commissioners, is apparently a substitute for any known dutiable article, or is apparently designed to evade duty, but possesses properties in the whole or in part which can be used or were intended to be applied for a similar purpose as such dutiable article, it shall be lawful for the governor to direct that a duty be levied on such article at a rate to be fixed in proportion to the degree in which such unknown article approximates in its qualities or uses to such dutiable article; and such rate thus fixed shall be published in a treasury order in the Gazette, and one other newspaper published in Sydney, and exhibited in the long room or other public place in the custom house, and a copy of all such treasury orders shall, without unnecessary delay, be laid before both houses of parliament.
That is a case in which, where no duty was fixed by statute, power was given by the legislature to the governor in council on the recommendation of the minister to fix a rate that bore some relation to the rate on the commodity to which it approximated in qualities or kind.
It was argued then, as it has been argued to-day, that the local legislature is in the nature of an agent or delegate, and, on the principle delegatus non potest delegare, the local legislature must exercise all its functions itself, and can delegate or intrust none of them to other persons or parties. But the judgment, after reciting that such had been the contention, goes on to say,	[DOT]
There is then a quotation from the judgment, and the court makes the clear statement that the tax in question had been imposed by the government and not by the legislature. The argument I heard yesterday in this chamber was that the scheme was a scheme prepared by individuals and not by this parliament. His lordship concludes:
It is argued that the tax in question has been imposed by the governor, and not by the legislature, who alone had power to impose it.
Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett

That is the argument here, that this parliament has the power and no one else. But the court dealt with it in these words:
But the duties levied under the order in council are really levied by the authority of the act under which the order is issued. The legislature has not parted with its perfect control over the governor, and has the power, of course, at any moment, of withdrawing or altering the power which they have entrusted to him. Under these circumstances their Lordships are of opinion that the judgment of the Supreme Court was wrong in declaring section^ 133 of the Customs Regulation Act of 1879 to be beyond the power of the legislature.
I merely mention these two cases because half a century has elapsed since the argument which has been advanced in this chamber so seriously and solemnly, and said to be of recent growth and development, was scotched by a judgment of the court in two cases. So far as the objection to this legislation on the ground that it is depriving parliament of its authority is concerned, we are met by two conclusive decisions which establish that that is not so. The right hon. gentleman realized his weakness in this regard yesterday when he stated that this was not for an emergency, it was forever. When I shook my head, he said: Well, until parliament repeals or amends it. That is the basis of all legislation, and that is what the court has said in both these cases. The power of parliament has not been taken away from it; you have not substituted for the power of parliament some other body or authority; you have merely' vested that power. Parliament has delegated for the present its powers to the board which it names, and until parliament withdraws that authority, the board may exercise that authority in the manner and to the extent indicated by the statute. So the first argument against this measure disappears. It disappears in the light of reason and of authority. Could anything be more monstrous than that this parliament could not delegate its powers to any body which it sees fit to set up?
During the nine years he was in power, the right hon. gentleman, with the help of "the birds" to his left, part of the time, and later with the help of the others, was dealing with this matter in various ways. First of all, there was the Canadian wheat board in 1922. The hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) dealt with that matter at length. In that case complete power was given by this parliament to a body to impose conditions on the export of wheat from the provinces. That board had power to make such regulations as it desired. Yesterday the right hon. gentle-

man referred to Russia, and referred to the nefarious institution called the government which sat opposite. He stated that there had never been granted by this parliament any power to the governor in council to impose embargoes. All one has to do is look at chapter 46 of the statutes of 1923. The right hon. gentleman enacted an amendment to the then Export Act to enable the governor in council to place an embargo against the export of pulpwood produced in this country. That is all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That is beside the question. The question is: Has the right hon. gentleman exercised the powers, never mind the extent to which they have been used? Has he enacted them in his own favour?
Then we pass to the Inland Water Freight Rates Act. I shall not go into the details of this legislation except to say that the board might prescribe the maximum rate. I shall pass on to 1925. I wonder how many hon. members of this house realize that a man cannot erect a building upon the right of way of the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National railways and undertake to store grain therein without a licence. That was passed in the house in 1925. To what board did they delegate authority to deal with the complex details of the grain trade, the largest single trade in this country? That power was delegated to the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada. Who gave them the power? This parliament. Who conferred it upon them? The government led by the right hon. gentleman and supported by the former Minister of Agriculture. As my colleague suggests, does parliament ever hear of what they are doing?
What about that great commission created to deal with freight rates, the board of railway commissioners? What about its delegated powers? What about the powers that this parliament conferred upon it to deal with freight rates? Do you first submit freight rates to this house and then tell the board afterwards, or has the board complete jurisdiction to deal with them? That board has as full and plenary powers as could be conferred upon it by parliament. It is true the right hon. gentleman's government did not pass the Railway Act. That was passed by one of his predecessors in office and subsequently consolidated under the government of Sir Robert Borden. The Canadian Farm Loan Act is another instance of delegated powers. Then there is the Domestic Fuel Act and the Vehicular Traffic Act. I take them one after

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
another, year after year. There is not one year that the right hon. gentleman was in office in this country that he did not ask this parliament to delegate some power and some authority to some body created by this parliament. That is the story that is written upon the statutes.
What do you mean by saying that this bill shall fail and is bad because parliament is delegating its powers to a body to be set up? It is true that that body may have its birth with the provincial authorities, but the central body which is to be set up is a body set up on the authority of this parliament. In order that constitutional difficulties may be overcome and that there may be an interrelationship between the functions and powers conferred by the provinces upon the local boards and the functions and powers to be exercised by the dominion board, adequate provisions have been made to meet just that situation.
Only last session we passed two statutes, one looking towards compositions under the authority of the Bankruptcy Act and the other dealing with the general powers of this parliament under section 91 of the British North America Act. Yesterday the supreme court sustained their validity by a unanimous judgment. There again you have an instance of the exercise of powers by this parliament to accomplish the purpose it has in mind.
I say to this house that if any hon. member is voting against this bill because he thinks that this parliament has no power to delegate its authority to any body which it sets up or which may otherwise be set up, he is voting contrary to the considered judgment of the court of last resort in the empire. But more, he is voting against something which was done by the government led by the right hon. gentleman opposite during every year of the nine years he held office.
One word more. It has been alleged that this legislation should fail-I really confess that I find it difficult to understand this- first, because it is socialistic; second, because it savours of sovietism, and third, because it savours of fascism. Those are the three grounds put forward why it should be rejected. I have dealt with the question of socialism and the socialistic tendencies of this legislation. As I read the history of the human race for the last twenty-five years, or even for the last fifteen years, I see more and more the tendency that the combined effort of all should assist the effort of one. This is so, whether or not we like it. I am no prophet, but I stand here to-night and say this, that you cannot read the history of our times
without realizing that more and more man is coming to a recognition of his obligations to his fellows, by banding himself together with his fellows for the purpose of promoting the welfare of each and all. That is the tendency of the times. You may stand out against it, as the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) did; you may object that it goes contrary to the doctrines of past centuries, as the hon. member for Ontario did; but we are dealing with conditions and not with theories, with actualities and with nothing else. We are dealing with conditions that have been forced upon the world in the hard school of experience, with conditions that have arisen in the light of the experience through which mankind has passed; and in the light of those conditions, and with that experience, there is not an hon. member of this house who reads, who observes, who takes the trouble to analyze, who does not realize that tendency, and a right tendency too. In these conditions that exist to-day, where you have such marked distinctions, such marked differences in fortunes, as old as the time of Aristotle, where you have changed conditions, the tendency is that the combined effort, by parliament or the legislature, as the case may be, by the majority, which means combination, shall be exercised for the welfare and good of each and all. That is the theory on which the world is now moving and is being governed.
I come next to the question of sovietism. Why, for the last twenty-five years in every province of this dominion there have been set up local boards, whether municipal councils or school districts, or a small combination of a few people for the purpose of taking goods to market by common understanding or on the authority of a statute. In the old province of Quebec it has been so-you have little local banks, savings institutions, the power to lend money one to another; and you had that long before the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Who has said this is compulsory? I am talking about something that is not compulsory; I am talking about free organization within the province of such units as I have indicated. I shall deal with the question of compulsion in a moment. Thus we have a clear understanding that there is nothing new in that respect, and to denounce as sovietism, because it sounds well, that which has been in existence for a third of a century at least in the older of the provinces, is to do violence to one's own understanding and intelligence.
Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett

Then we come to the third ground. Section 9 of the act confers upon the government power to erect and create boards within districts and areas to be indicated. Now, this act is intended to be of use; it is not ornamental like the inland freight bill. It is intended to be of some use to the country; it is intended to serve a purpose, and I am going to put this to the house to-night:	There is
a rule of our jurisprudence, one of the most important that we have-So use your own as not to injure your neighbour's. That is the rule; and if you bring upon your property anything that causes injury to your neighbour, though it be surrounded by all the skill and care that engineering judgment would suggest, nevertheless if injury accrues by reason of your having brought any such thing on your property you are liable for damages.
Now transfer that broad principle to our economic life. Shall farmers who are looking to governments for light and leading, for assistance in the marketing of their products, be told that in a surfeited market, under the conditions to which I have alluded, by reason of the war-are they to be told that any man can ship any product he likes into a market already surfeited and so destroy the price of all products? Is that just? Is that right? Every member of this house who votes against the bill wants to declare that that is right, that it is right for one man, the minority as the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard) says, notwithstanding that there may be ninety-nine out of one hundred who think otherwise, by shipping his product to such a market, to destroy the price and the market and leave his neighbour ruthlessly ruined, without caring for the consequences.
Well, that is not the law of the country, and this statute is passed for the purpose of seeing that it shall not be the law with respect to associations. That is the purpose of the measure. When one heard the argument adduced yesterday, that the effect of this bill would be to enable the government, ruthlessly and autocratically, to do as it pleased with respect to these matters, one had only to put this to oneself. The central board, acting in association with the other boards, the local boards, for the purpose of securing to them the maximum return for their products, may be confronted with a situation in which a small, or even a larger area may take no action, doing nothing for the common good; and parliament has said that under those circumstances its will shall prevail. That is all. And why should it not? What about your county councils, your legislatures and parlia-fMr. Bennett.]
ments? The will of the majority prevails; but it is suggested here that the government will ruthlessly and arrogantly do something that will be at variance with the good of the whole community. Governments sometimes commit suicide, so the opposition say. But be that as it may, is it likely that they will consciously do so? When we are dealing with legislation of this character, as the privy council has so often said, we must adopt one cardinal rule, and that is, that it must be assumed that the legislators were acting for the common good in passing legislation, and not for destruction, not ruthlessly to destroy and ruin but to promote and upbuild and further the welfare of all. And that power in this bill is intended to prevent that reluctant minority, to whom the hon. member for Kamouraska refers, from destroying the efficiency and effectiveness of this measure.

I have not suggested
that there was. What I am suggesting is this. Apparently the opposition have one object in mind. It makes no difference what legislation is introduced by this government, they oppose it, no matter what it is. There are exceptions to that rale. I wonder how many hon. gentlemen realized, as I did the mental agony of the ex-Minister of Agriculture

and I say that in no scoffing sense, for I have been through it. I voted in 1913 against my party, I spoke against it, in connection with the acquisition of railways; and I know how one feels if he has been a minister, and has worried and thought and then concluded, that he must serve his country and not his party.
Will any hon. gentleman in this house show that the attitude of the opposition has not been one of consistent and persistent opposition since this depression began? What measures have we offered to this house which they have not, by every means in their power, endeavoured to frustrate and destroy? And here is one of the reasons why, I suggest, this legislation is being so fought-and I use the word advisedly. What is there in this bill that justifies the long debates that have taken place over it? What is there in the bill to justify hearing the same speech three times? What is there in it to justify listening to talk about the trade and commerce of the country before the depression and afterwards, and a comparison of the two? What have been the relevancy of the observa-

Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
tions and the character of the opposition? Why has there been such opposition? Why? Because in this bill there is a provision that, if it were not there, might render the bill futile and useless; because we have inserted in it a provision that makes it no longer possible for the vociferous and vocal minority to destroy the efficiency and effectiveness of the legislation, we are met with cries that this is in derogation of the rights of parliament, a frustration of the power of the will of the people through their chosen representatives. We are told further that this is an effort at fascism on the one hand and sovietism on the other.
One word more. The right hon. gentleman yesterday denounced this bill and clause 12 has been denounced in this chamber as having behind it a hidden purpose. He says that there is behind it a vast scheme of economic imperialism. I ask any thoughtful member of the house whether he thinks that is a worthy criticism with respect to legislation of this character. All hon. members know that in all parts of the country the word "imperialism " by reason of the thought in the minds of many connotes military power and despotism as in the days of Rome, Baby-Ion and Assyria. That word will promote prejudices, create animosities and antipathies in certain sections of the country. When every other argument fails and is forgotten my right hon. friend cries aloud:	This is
imperialism! Only a few short months ago in the city of Quebec the right hon. gentleman made this observation; listen to these words:
This is an issue of vast import and significance and the resurrection of an old issue, most of us thought dead and buried long ago. Whether the British commonwealth of nations shall be permitted to remain what it has become, and what it is now-a community of free nations owing allegiance to a common sovereign-and to continue to expand on these lines, or whether it is to lose its identity and the individuality of its component selfgoverning parts and be made to model the Babylonian, Assyrian, Macedonian, Turkish, Roman and the German empires.
There you have the leader of the opposition at his best and his worst. There is the demagogue on the one hand appealing to the prejudices and passions of those whose antipathy to military empires is well known, and on the other seeking the opportunity to get a few votes.

Just so, but my hon.
friend's leader is not. That is the point exactly. Have I been talking imperialism with respect to these agreements? I have said in every country, I have said in Great Britain itself, that whatever w'e did with



Marketing Act-Mr. Bennett
respect to Britain and other portions of the empire, our first duty was to Canada. I said that everywhere; I said it in London; I say it in Canada and I say that when the members of the family desire to get together and promote their common fortunes, it ill becomes any man to scoff, by talking about imperialism, at the successful results of their efforts.
Let me go a step further; it does not stop just there. During the last election I was charged with having been too pro-Canadian. If the newspaper reports are correct as to what the right hon. gentleman said at Barrie, he said that he was for Great Britain, and wherever the word "British" appeared either in the original of his public address or in the press of the province in which it was made, you always found that note, but you find it no more. He thinks that because this country has made trade agreements with Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain, the Irish Free State, India and South Africa, because of the agreements we have made within our own empire, we are thus to be branded with "imperialism". Mr. Bruce pointed out-and no one has denied this,-and the right hon. gentleman said that with what Mr. Bruce said he was in accord-that there is left but one country in which in the main the products of the rest of the empire might find a market. That is what he said, and it is because we have that market and a preference in it; it is because the dream of Sir Wilfrid Laurier as approved by his own people and himself in the conference of 1897 and because the dream of Sir Lomer Gouin, Mr. Graham and the right hon. gentleman himself in 1923 failed of realization and is now come true, they must oppose that which they formerly advocated.
I said in this chamber, standing in the place where my right hon. friend now is, that the greatest service Canada could make to the British Empire was to develop that part of the empire called Canada. I said that a woollen mill in Canada was as valuable an asset to the British Empire as a woollen mill in Yorkshire. I said that in my speech delivered on the budget in 1930, the year of the election. I said it when other nations were closing their doors to us, and let it be remembered that in the nine years that elapsed during which the right hon. gentleman and his followers were in power every one of those markets, one after another, was closed to us. Then they said: What about your trade treaties? We made a trade treaty with Great Britain. When we came into power a trade treaty with New Zealand was terminated, and we made a new one. We made treaties with Australia, South

Africa, the Irish Free State and Germany. During the nine years hon. gentlemen opposite were in power efforts to make a treaty with Germany on somewhat similar terms failed; we succeeded. A treaty was made with Austria. We are now about to negotiate a treaty with Poland. During all these months since 1930 we have been carrying on continuously, within the ambit of our powers and under the conditions that existed, negotiations with the great republic to the south. We completed a new treaty, through the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), with the republic of France, and all this in spite of the fact that we had to face a condition we did not create but which was inherited, with the markets of these countries closed against us through the actions taken while hon. gentlemen opposite were in office.
Will any hon. gentlemen rise in their places and say that is not so? Can they stand in their places over there and say that from the time they came into office in the fall of 1921 or the spring of 1922 until 1930, when they went out of office, during all that time the nations of the world did not consistently raise their tariffs against Canada? Although we turned the other cheek twice, as Senator Dandurand said at the League of Nations in Geneva; although the leader of our government coaxed us not to say anything that might provoke our great neighbour to the south, we were shut out of those markets by the highest tariffs we have ever had to face in that country, and all the nations of the world refused to accept our commerce. Then we turned, as the great chief of the Liberal party saw we would, to that greatest of all consuming markets to which all producing people look, and we secured there a preference that is now condemned and denounced in this house as imperialism. Go and tell the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), who voted for those preferences, that what he has been voting for is crude material and economic imperialism.
Go and tell those who have reaped benefits to the extent of $11,000,000 or $12,000,000, as against their position if duties had to be paid, that this is not to their benefit or for their welfare. Why this should be brought into this debate is hard to understand ; there can be but one excuse and one reason, an effort to draw a red herring across the trail, to consolidate a broken party, to keep together men of differing views, some thinking one way and some the other; to get them all together to vote against the bill, to hold them at any cost so that the world may not know the dissen-

Marketing Act-Mr. Ralston
sions that have characterized their deliberations with regard to this matter.
Let them vote to-night. In a few minutes we will give them the opportunity to vote, and after they have done so let them remember that they have voted against, according to the agrarians and producers of primary products, that measure of assistance that is not denied to the other leg of the great movement that will make for the prosperity of the world. Secretary Wallace said the other day that Labour was the one leg and agriculture the other; as they march forward sometimes one and then the other is in advance, but if they march together there comes prosperity. So now are we to deny the one and accede to the other; grant to the one and deny the other? Hon. gentlemen opposite do not desire that there should be placed upon the statute books of this country a measure giving the primary producer an opportunity to receive that measure of assistance, that measure of parliamentary aid, that should come to him as the producer of the natural wealth of the country, that this country may recover and ultimately prosper as it did in days gone by.
Sir. I have trespassed somewhat longer upon the time of the house than I had intended. There are other matters that might be dealt with, but I trust that I have said sufficient to indicate the shallowness of the arguments that have been made against this measure. I have quoted the authorities of the courts of last resort to show that arguments of that kind are not valid, and I commend this bill to this house. I do so because the bill affords a practical illustration of the efforts that have been made by a party not bound by the shibboleths of the past, but accepting only the history of the past for the purpose of guiding them aright in the pathways they hew out for the future. I commend the bill also because we believe that the true measure of faith of the Conservative party is shown by our ability and willingness to accept, in the light of experience and knowledge, those principles which we know are sound and which involve, as they do, the lopping off of much that has gone before in order that the world may progress and civilization prevail.
